data.title: Q1.1: Malignant Melanoma (Classification, Clinical Features, Prognostic Factors, Staging & Management)

children.title: Malignant tumour of melanocytes
children.detail: A malignant tumour of melanocytes (cells of neural crest origin located in the basal epidermis).

children.title: Sites
children.detail: It can arise in skin, mucosa, retina, and leptomeninges.

children.title: Accounts for <5% of skin malignancies but causes >75% of skin cancer-related deaths
Commonest cancer in young adults (20-39 years)
Ultraviolet radiation (UVR)
children.detail: Especially intense intermittent "flash-fry" exposure.

children.title: Immunosuppression
children.detail: Increases risk 20-30-fold.

children.title: Macroscopic Features Suggestive of Malignant Change in Naevi (ABCDE / Summary Box 45.5)
Elevation / Thickness
children.detail: Nodularity or ulceration.

children.title: Tingling / itching / serosanguineous discharge
children.detail: Late signs.

children.title: Usually arises in a pre-existing naevus after years of slow radial change followed by rapid vertical growth (nodularity)
Arises de novo
children.detail: More common in middle-aged men on trunk/head/neck.

children.title: Lacks a radial growth phase
children.detail: Vertical growth from the outset.

children.title: Arises from Hutchinson's melanotic freckle (melanoma in situ) on sun-damaged face/neck/hands of elderly patients (women > men)
Slowest to enter vertical growth phase
Acral Lentiginous Melanoma (ALM - 2-8% in whites, 35-60% in Asian/African/Hispanic populations)
Affects glabrous skin of palms, soles, and nail beds (subungual)
Pigmentation of the proximal/lateral nail fold widening into a triangular macule with nail dystrophy
children.detail: Diagnostic of subungual melanoma.

children.title: Amelanotic melanoma
children.detail: Flesh-coloured, poor prognosis due to late diagnosis.

children.title: Desmoplastic melanoma
children.detail: Head/neck, propensity for perineural infiltration and local recurrence.

children.title: Horizontal (Radial) Growth Phase
children.detail: Atypical melanocytes spread laterally along the dermoepidermal junction.

children.title: Vertical Growth Phase
children.detail: Invasion deep into the dermis; confers metastatic potential.

children.title: 1. Breslow Thickness (Most important prognostic indicator in Stage I / Node-negative disease)
Measured vertically with an ocular micrometer to the nearest 0.1 mm from the top of the stratum granulosum to the deepest point of tumour invasion
Level I: Confined to epidermis (in situ)
Level II: Invasion into papillary dermis
Level III: Filling papillary dermis up to the papillary-reticular dermal interface
Level IV: Invasion into reticular dermis
Level V: Invasion into subcutaneous fat
Regional lymph node metastasis
children.detail: Single most important overall prognostic index; once clinically involved, 70-85% have occult distant metastases.

children.title: T1 (<= 1.0 mm; T1a <0.8 mm without ulceration)
Full-thickness excision biopsy with a 2-3 mm clinical margin of skin and a cuff of subdermal fat
Incision biopsy is only done for very large facial/acral lesions where complete excision is disfiguring
2. Wide Local Excision (WLE) Margins (Definitive Local Control)
Clinically Node-Negative (cN0)
children.detail: Offer Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) for tumours T2a (>1.0 mm) and above (or >0.8 mm with ulceration).

children.title: Clinically Node-Positive or Positive SLNB
children.detail: Therapeutic/Completion regional lymphadenectomy.

children.title: BRAF V600 inhibitors (Dabrafenib, Vemurafenib) combined with MEK inhibitor (Trametinib) for the 50% of melanomas harbouring BRAF mutations

data.title: Q1.2: Basal Cell Carcinoma (Rodent Ulcer) & Mohs Micrographic Surgery

children.title: Slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumour of pluripotential epithelial cells arising from the basal layer of the epidermis and outer root sheath of hair follicles
Affects pilosebaceous skin; never occurs on palms/soles
Commonest skin malignancy in white-skinned populations (outnumbers SCC by 4:1)
95% occur between ages 40 and 80 years; males > females
Gorlin's syndrome
children.detail: PTCH1 gene mutation on Chr 9q.

children.title: Nodular / Nodulocystic
children.detail: Translucent, pearly nodule with surface telangiectasia; central necrosis produces a classic "Rodent Ulcer" with a rolled, beaded edge.

children.title: Cystic
children.detail: Large cystic spaces.

children.title: Pigmented
children.detail: Contains melanin; mimics malignant melanoma.

children.title: Superficial (Multifocal / Superficial spreading)
children.detail: Erythematous scaly plaques, often on the trunk.

children.title: Infiltrative (Morphoeic, Ice-pick, Cicatrising)
children.detail: Synthesises type IV collagenase, leading to rapid, ill-defined subclinical spread with scar-like plaques.

children.title: Nests of ovoid basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm and a characteristic peripheral "palisading" single layer of columnar nuclei
Only the outer layer actively divides
High-risk embryonic fusion planes ("H-zone" of face: periorbital, nose, ear - risk of cranial invasion)
Excision under loupe magnification with a 4 mm peripheral margin for well-defined low-risk lesions (2-15 mm depending on macroscopic variant)
Reconstruction via primary closure, skin graft, or local flaps
Principle
children.detail: Serial horizontal/tangential excision of skin cancer with immediate 100% microscopic mapping of frozen-section margins by a dermatological surgeon before defect reconstruction.

children.title: Lesions in tissue-sparing sites (eyelids, nasal tip, periauricular)
Radiotherapy
children.detail: Reserved for elderly/infirm patients (similar recurrence rates to surgery, but risks radiation-induced malignancy 10-20 years later).

children.title: Topical Therapy
children.detail: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) or Imiquimod (immune response modifier) for biopsy-proven superficial BCCs.

children.title: Cryotherapy / Curettage & Cautery
children.detail: For small, low-risk superficial lesions.

data.title: Q1.3: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) & Marjolin's Ulcer

children.title: Malignant tumour of keratinising cells of the epidermis (stratum spinosum/basalis) or its appendages
Actinic (Solar) Keratosis
children.detail: Sun-damaged dyskeratotic scaly plaques; up to 20% progress to SCC.

children.title: Cutaneous Horn
children.detail: Hyperkeratotic projection where height > base diameter (10% harbour underlying SCC at the base).

children.title: Keratoacanthoma
children.detail: Rapidly growing dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug; now classified as a well-differentiated, self-healing variant of SCC (excision recommended).

children.title: Bowen's Disease (SCC in situ)
children.detail: Slowly enlarging erythematous, crusted plaque (full-thickness epidermal atypia). On the glans penis, it is termed Erythroplasia of Queyrat. Treated with topical 5-FU, Imiquimod, or 4 mm surgical excision.

children.title: Macroscopic
children.detail: Verrucous, papillomatous, or ulcerated lesion with a characteristic heaped-up, everted edge and indurated base.

children.title: Irregular masses of atypical squamous cells invading the dermis with keratin pearls (epithelial nests)
Graded by Broders' Histological Grading based on the proportion of undifferentiated cells
Depth >2 mm (>6 mm has 15% metastasis rate)
Tumour >2 cm (or high-risk): 1 cm clearance margin (or Mohs micrographic surgery)
Regional Nodes
children.detail: Ultrasound/FNAC of palpable nodes; therapeutic lymph node dissection (with adjuvant radiotherapy if multiple nodes or extracapsular spread).

children.title: Definition
children.detail: A well-differentiated but locally aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic unstable scar, burn wound, chronic venous ulcer, or osteomyelitis sinus tract.

children.title: Painless
children.detail: Devoid of nerve fibrils due to surrounding dense scar fibrosis.

children.title: Slow-growing & Initially Lymph-node negative
children.detail: Scar fibrosis obliterates local lymphatic channels; however, once it breaches the scar bed into normal tissue, it metastasises rapidly with a poor prognosis.

children.title: Clinical Suspicion
children.detail: Foul-smelling discharge, raised everted edge, or fungating growth appearing in a longstanding scar/ulcer.

children.title: Wedge biopsy from the edge to confirm diagnosis
Wide local excision with a 1-2 cm margin + skin grafting/flap cover (or amputation if underlying bone is invaded)

data.title: Q1.4: Classification of Ulcers

children.title: A discontinuity of an epithelial surface characterised by progressive destruction of surface epithelium and a granulating base
Surrounding skin is inflamed and oedematous
Floor is covered with profuse offensive slough without healthy granulation tissue
Draining lymph nodes are enlarged and tender
Floor has healthy pink/red granular tissue with serous discharge
Inner red zone of vascular granulation
Middle bluish zone of growing epithelium
Floor contains pale, avascular granulation tissue
Base and edge are heavily indurated and fibrosed
Shows no tendency towards healing (e.g., chronic venous ulcer)
Traumatic
children.detail: Mechanical (dental ulcer of tongue), physical (electrical/radiation), or chemical.

children.title: Venous
children.detail: Gravitational ulcer in the gaiter area.

children.title: Arterial (Ischaemic)
children.detail: Atherosclerosis, Buerger's disease.

children.title: Neuropathic (Trophic / Perforating)
children.detail: Diabetic neuropathy, tabes dorsalis, leprosy, spina bifida.

children.title: Metabolic & Tropical
children.detail: Diabetes mellitus, tropical phagedenic ulcer, pyoderma gangrenosum, cryoglobulinaemia.

children.title: Specific Infective Ulcers
children.detail: Tuberculosis, syphilis (hard chancre, gummatous ulcer), actinomycosis, Meleney's ulcer.

children.title: Malignant Ulcers
children.detail: Squamous cell carcinoma, Basal cell carcinoma (Rodent ulcer), Malignant melanoma, Marjolin's ulcer.

children.title: Sloping (Shelving) Edge
children.detail: Healing non-specific or venous ulcers.

children.title: Punched-Out Edge
children.detail: Deep vertical edge seen in tertiary syphilitic gumma, trophic/neuropathic ulcers, and ischaemic ulcers.

children.title: Undermined Edge
children.detail: Tuberculous ulcer (infection spreads faster in subcutaneous fat than in overlying skin) and Pyoderma gangrenosum (purple undermined edge).

children.title: Rolled (Beaded) Edge
children.detail: Basal cell carcinoma (Rodent ulcer).

children.title: Everted (Heaped-Up) Edge
children.detail: Squamous cell carcinoma / adenocarcinoma (rapidly proliferating malignant cells spill over normal skin).

children.title: Grade 0: Pre-ulcerative lesion / high-risk foot with bony deformity
Grade 1: Superficial ulcer involving full skin thickness only
Grade 2: Deep ulcer penetrating to ligaments, tendons, or joint capsule (no abscess/osteomyelitis)
Grade 3: Deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis
Grade 4: Localised gangrene of forefoot or heel
Grade 5: Extensive gangrene of the entire foot

data.title: Q1.5: High-Yield Short Answers in Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue

children.title: Retention cyst lined by true stratified squamous epithelium derived from the hair follicle infundibulum (or traumatic implantation)
Contains cheesy, foul-smelling keratinaceous material (not sebum)
Derive from the external root sheath
Smooth, firm, spherical swelling fixed to the skin
Characteristic central bluish/black punctum (blocked duct opening)
Occurs anywhere except palms and soles
Ulceration
children.detail: Cock's peculiar tumour — granulating infected scalp cyst mimicking SCC.

children.title: Complete surgical excision of the cyst along with its entire capsule/wall and an elliptical wedge of skin containing the punctum
If infected / abscessed
children.detail: Initial incision and drainage (or avulsion) followed by formal excision once inflammation subsides.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: An infective gangrene of the skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by Staphylococcus aureus, consisting of multiple communicating furuncles (boils) draining through multiple sieve-like openings on the skin.

children.title: Predominantly affects middle-aged/elderly diabetics or immunocompromised patients
Commonest site is the nape of the neck and back (hairy, thick skin with poor vascularity)
Starts as a painful, indurated, dusky-red swelling
Softens centrally into a honeycombed slough ("cribriform appearance") discharging pus
Heals leaving a deep crateriform ulcer
Surgical cruciate incision and debridement of all necrotic slough and loculi
Followed by daily packing and secondary healing or split-skin grafting
3. Keloid vs Hypertrophic Scar [KU 24, 21, RGU] (Table surgery-tbl-001)
Hypertrophic Scar
children.detail: Raised scar that remains strictly within the confines of the original wound.

children.title: Keloid Scar
children.detail: Claw-like proliferation of immature collagen that extends beyond the original wound margins into normal skin.

children.title: Hypertrophic Scar
children.detail: Non-familial; no racial predisposition.

children.title: Keloid Scar
children.detail: Genetic predisposition; commoner in darker skin types (African/Asian).

children.title: Hypertrophic Scar
children.detail: Appears within weeks of injury; improves/regresses spontaneously over 6–12 months.

children.title: Keloid Scar
children.detail: May appear months after trivial trauma; continues to grow progressively and rarely regresses.

children.title: Hypertrophic Scar
children.detail: Across flexor surfaces and lines of skin tension.

children.title: Keloid Scar
children.detail: Presternal region, deltoid, earlobe, face, and neck.

children.title: Hypertrophic Scar
children.detail: Responds well to silicone gel sheeting, compression garments, and intralesional steroids.

children.title: Keloid Scar
children.detail: High recurrence rate (>50%) after simple excision; treated with intralesional Triamcinolone acetonide, compression, or intralesional excision + adjuvant low-dose radiotherapy.

children.title: Vascular Tumours (Haemangiomas)
children.detail: Endothelial hyperplasia.

children.title: Vascular Malformations
children.detail: Normal endothelial turnover; structural errors.

children.title: Present at or shortly after birth; female:male = 3:1
Rapid proliferation in the first year followed by slow involution ("70% resolve by age 7")
Capillary Haemangioma (Strawberry Naevus)
children.detail: Bright red, raised, compressible lesion on head/neck.

children.title: Large lesions can trap platelets causing consumptive thrombocytopenia (Kasabach–Merritt Syndrome)
Present at birth; grow proportionately with the child; never involute
Salmon patch (nape of neck; fades by 1 year)
Port-Wine Stain
children.detail: Purple macule in V1/V2 trigeminal dermatomes; associated with Sturge–Weber syndrome; treated with Pulsed-Dye Laser.

data.title: Q2.1: Pathophysiology, Assessment, Classification & Management of Major Thermal Burns

children.title: Covers KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 17, 16, 15 — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers
Zone of Coagulation
children.detail: Central area of irreversible coagulative necrosis at the point of maximum heat transfer.

children.title: Zone of Stasis
children.detail: Surrounding area of decreased tissue perfusion; potentially salvageable with prompt cooling and fluid resuscitation, otherwise progresses to necrosis.

children.title: Zone of Hyperaemia
children.detail: Outer zone of vasodilation due to inflammatory mediators; recovers fully.

children.title: Systemic Inflammatory & Circulatory Shock Response (Summary Box 46.6)

Thermal protein alteration and pain fibres trigger complement activation, neuropeptide release, and Hageman factor (Factor XII) activation (driving arachidonic acid, thrombin, and kallikrein cascades)
Massive systemic capillary permeability occurs in burns >15% TBSA in adults (>10% in children)
Shift of water, electrolytes, and plasma proteins into the interstitial space → hypovolaemic burn shock and generalized oedema
History of fire in an enclosed space
Supraglottic Upper Airway Thermal Injury
children.detail: Inhaled hot gases cause progressive laryngeal oedema within 4–24 hours → life-threatening airway obstruction.

children.title: Subglottic Lower Airway Injury (Chemical Pneumonitis)
children.detail: Inhaled smoke particles and steam cause sloughing of respiratory epithelium, fibrin casts, and ARDS (peaks at 24 hours to 5 days).

children.title: Carbon monoxide (CO) binds haemoglobin with 250 times the affinity of oxygen (forming carboxyhaemoglobin) and inhibits cytochrome oxidase
Hydrogen cyanide (from burning plastics/polymers) binds ferric iron (Fe³⁺) in mitochondrial cytochrome a_3
Splanchnic vasoconstriction → mucosal ischaemia (Curling's ulcer), ileus, bacterial translocation, and abdominal compartment syndrome
Suppression of cell-mediated immunity and hypermetabolic catabolic drive
2. Assessment of Area (TBSA) & Classification of Burn Depth
Assessment of Percentage Total Body Surface Area (% TBSA)
Palmar Surface Method
children.detail: Patient's palm and fingers (distal wrist crease to fingertips) = ~1% TBSA (useful for small/patchy burns <10%).

children.title: Clinical Scenario Calculation [KU 24 / TU]
children.detail: Head & neck [9%] + Both upper limbs [18%] + Front & back of chest [9% + 9% = 18%] = 45% TBSA; if abdomen [9%] is also included = 54% TBSA.

children.title: Modified Lund and Browder Chart
children.detail: Most accurate method, mandatory in children (at birth: head is 18% and each lower limb is 13.5%; for each year up to age 10, subtract 1% from the head and add 0.5% to each leg).

children.title: Classification by Depth of Burn (Table surgery-tbl-002)
Histological Level
children.detail: Epidermis only.

children.title: Clinical Appearance, Blanching & Sensation
children.detail: Erythematous, dry, no blisters; brisk capillary refill; painful.

children.title: Healing Time & Scarring
children.detail: Heals in 5–7 days without scarring.

children.title: Histological Level
children.detail: Up to Papillary Dermis.

children.title: Clinical Appearance, Blanching & Sensation
children.detail: Thin-walled blisters; underlying dermis is pink, moist, and weeping; blanches briskly on pressure; hyperaesthetic (very painful to pinprick).

children.title: Healing Time & Scarring
children.detail: Heals spontaneously within 14 days via adnexal structures without scarring.

children.title: Histological Level
children.detail: Reticular Dermis.

children.title: Clinical Appearance, Blanching & Sensation
children.detail: Dry/pale or mottled cherry-red dermis (fixed capillary staining); does not blanch; reduced sensation (cannot distinguish sharp from blunt pinprick).

children.title: Healing Time & Scarring
children.detail: Takes >3 weeks to heal; leads to severe hypertrophic scarring; requires tangential excision & grafting.

children.title: Histological Level
children.detail: Entire dermis destroyed (into subcutis).

children.title: Clinical Appearance, Blanching & Sensation
children.detail: Hard, dry, waxy-white, leathery or charred black eschar; visible thrombosed subcutaneous veins; no blanching; completely anaesthetic to pinprick.

children.title: Healing Time & Scarring
children.detail: Cannot heal spontaneously except from margins; requires excision & split-skin grafting.

children.title: 3. Management of a Major Burn Patient (e.g., 60% TBSA Burn)
Stop the burning process ("Stop, Drop, and Roll")
Cool the burn with running tepid tap water (15°C for 20 minutes, effective up to 1 hour post-burn; avoid ice/hypothermia)
A – Airway with Cervical Spine Control
children.detail: Inspect for signs of inhalational injury. Early elective endotracheal intubation is mandatory for suspected airway burns before laryngeal oedema obliterates the airway (within 4–24 hours).

children.title: 100% high-flow humidified oxygen (reduces half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin from 4 hours to 40 minutes)
If cyanide toxicity is suspected, give intravenous Hydroxocobalamin (Vitamin B12)
Nebulised heparin, N-acetylcysteine (mucolytic), and salbutamol (albuterol) for smoke inhalation
Chest Escharotomy if circumferential full-thickness torso eschar restricts chest excursion
C – Circulation
children.detail: Insert two wide-bore (14G/16G) IV cannulae (through unburned skin if possible), send baseline bloods (FBC, U&E, clotting, lactate, ABG, COHb, group & crossmatch), and insert a Foley urinary catheter to monitor hourly urine output.

children.title: D – Disability
children.detail: Assess GCS (rule out hypoxia, CO poisoning, or head trauma).

children.title: E – Exposure & Environmental Control
children.detail: Remove all jewellery/clothing, assess TBSA, and prevent hypothermia (warmed IV fluids, Bair Hugger, warm room >28°C).

children.title: F – Fluid Resuscitation (Indicated for >15% TBSA in adults; >10% TBSA in children)
Modified Parkland Formula (Crystalloid)
children.detail: Total Fluid in first 24 hours = 4 mL × Body Weight (kg) × % TBSA Burned (Using Ringer's Lactate / Hartmann's solution).

children.title: Rate of Administration
children.detail: Give 50% in the first 8 hours (calculated from the time of the burn injury, not arrival) and the remaining 50% over the next 16 hours.

children.title: Example Calculation (60% burn in a 60 kg patient)
children.detail: 4 × 60 × 60 = 14,400 mL (7,200 mL in first 8 hours; 7,200 mL over next 16 hours).

children.title: Children
children.detail: Add maintenance dextrose-saline (100 mL/kg for first 10 kg + 50 mL/kg for next 10 kg + 20 mL/kg for each kg >20 kg).

children.title: Muir and Barclay Formula (Colloid alternative after 12h)
children.detail: (0.5 × Weight (kg) × % TBSA/1) = 1 ration of Human Albumin Solution given in 6 rations over 36 hours (three 4-hourly, two 6-hourly, one 12-hourly).

children.title: Monitoring Resuscitation
children.detail: Formulae are only a starting guide; titrate fluids dynamically to maintain Urine Output of 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hour in adults (1–2 mL/kg/hour in children).

children.title: Analgesia
children.detail: Titrated intravenous morphine (avoid IM route due to unpredictable absorption in shock).

children.title: Nutrition
children.detail: For burns ≥ 20% TBSA, insert a nasogastric or nasojejunal tube and start enteral feeding within 6 hours to prevent gut mucosal atrophy and bacterial translocation.

children.title: Ulcer & DVT Prophylaxis
children.detail: Proton pump inhibitors (for Curling's ulcer), LMWH, and tetanus prophylaxis.

children.title: Indication
children.detail: Circumferential full-thickness burns of the limbs (causing tourniquet-like ischaemia) or chest wall (causing mechanical respiratory restriction).

children.title: Incise full thickness of burned eschar into subcutaneous fat using cutting diathermy
Chest
children.detail: Longitudinal incisions along anterior axillary lines joined by transverse incisions below the clavicles and across the costal margin/xiphisternum.

children.title: Upper Limb
children.detail: Mid-axial incisions (passing anterior to the medial epicondyle at the elbow to protect the ulnar nerve).

children.title: Lower Limb
children.detail: Mid-axial incisions (passing posterior to the medial malleolus to spare the long saphenous vein, and anterior to the fibular head to spare the common peroneal nerve).

children.title: 2. Group A (Superficial Partial-Thickness) Wound Care
children.detail: Cleanse, debride ruptured blisters, and apply biological/biosynthetic dressings (Biobrane), hydrocolloids (Duoderm), silicone sheets (Mepitel), or nanocrystalline silver dressings (Acticoat).

children.title: 3. Group B (Deep Partial-Thickness & Full-Thickness) Excision & Grafting
Early Tangential Excision (Watson's knife / Humby knife)
children.detail: Shave necrotic burn layers sequentially until brisk punctate dermal/fat bleeding is reached (exploiting the anaesthetic, haemodynamic, and bacterial windows within 48–72 hours). Blood loss is minimised using tourniquets and subcutaneous tumescence with 1:500,000 adrenaline.

children.title: Silver sulphadiazine + Cerium nitrate
children.detail: Forms a sterile leathery eschar and boosts cell-mediated immunity.

children.title: 5% Mafenide acetate
children.detail: Penetrates eschar/cartilage well; side effect: carbonic anhydrase inhibition causing metabolic acidosis.

children.title: Autologous Split-Thickness Skin Grafts (STSG)
children.detail: Sheet grafts for face/hands/neck; meshed 1:1.5 to 1:6 or Meek micrografting for extensive burns.

children.title: If TBSA >50% and donor sites are insufficient
children.detail: Use temporary cadaveric allografts or dermal matrices (Integra or Biodegradable Temporising Matrix [BTM]).

children.title: Physiotherapy & Splinting
children.detail: Start from Day 1; splint hands in the position of safe immobilisation (intrinsic-plus), neck in extension, and axillae in 90° abduction.

children.title: Hypertrophic Scar Management
children.detail: Custom-fitted pressure garments (worn 23 hours/day for 6–18 months), topical silicone gel sheets, intralesional steroid injections, and antipruritics.

children.title: Surgical Release of Contractures
children.detail: Z-plasty or multiple Y-to-V advancement flaps for linear scar bands; incision + full-thickness skin graft (FTSG), dermal substitutes, tissue expansion (especially for post-burn scalp alopecia), or free flaps for broad contractures. Urgent eyelid release + grafting if ectropion threatens exposure keratitis.

data.title: Q2.2: Electrical and Chemical Burns

children.title: Classified into Low-Voltage (<1000 V) and High-Voltage (>1000 V) injuries
Alternating current causes muscle tetany ("let-go phenomenon"), locking the victim's hand onto the source and causing deep local contact burns in the fingers with underlying nerve/tendon damage
Systemic Danger
children.detail: Disrupts normal cardiac pacing → ventricular fibrillation / cardiac arrest without direct myocardial necrosis.

children.title: Direct Current Conduction (victim acts as a conductor to earth)
Pathophysiology ("Iceberg Effect")
children.detail: Small, charred entry and exit wounds mask massive deep myonecrosis along neurovascular bundles and bone (bone has the highest electrical resistance and generates intense heat, cooking surrounding deep muscle bellies).

children.title: Acute Compartment Syndrome
children.detail: Rapid muscle swelling within intact fascia.

children.title: Rhabdomyolysis & Myoglobinuria
children.detail: Massive release of myoglobin causes dark "port-wine" urine and acute tubular necrosis / renal failure.

children.title: Severe Metabolic Acidosis and associated fractures/spinal injuries from blast propulsion
Aggressive Fluid Resuscitation
children.detail: Maintain a higher target urine output of 1.5–2.0 mL/kg/hour (using Hartmann's solution + sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine and mannitol to flush myoglobin casts).

children.title: Urgent Decompressive Fasciotomy (not just escharotomy) of affected limb compartments, serial surgical debridement of necrotic muscle, or primary amputation if the limb is unsalvageable
Pathophysiology
children.detail: Damage occurs via local tissue corrosion/protein denaturation and systemic toxicity from absorption.

children.title: Acids
children.detail: Cause coagulative necrosis, forming a coagulum/eschar that limits deeper penetration.

children.title: Alkalis (Cement, Lime, Bleach, Drain cleaners)
children.detail: Cause liquefactive necrosis and saponification of fats, allowing deeper, progressive tissue destruction (far more dangerous, especially in ocular injuries).

children.title: Brush off any dry solid chemical powders first (e.g., elemental sodium, white phosphorus)
Immediate, Copious Water Lavage for 30–60 minutes
children.detail: Dilutes and washes away the agent; do not attempt to neutralise with an opposite chemical as the exothermic reaction worsens thermal injury.

children.title: HF chelates tissue calcium and magnesium, causing excruciating pain, deep necrosis, and potentially fatal systemic hypocalcaemia and cardiac arrhythmias
Treated with topical 10% Calcium Gluconate gel, local infiltration, or intra-arterial / intravenous Bier's block with Calcium Gluconate (and urgent excision if concentration >50%)

data.title: Q3.1: Skin Grafts (Types, Split-Skin Graft / Thiersch Graft, Full-Thickness / Wolfe Graft)

children.title: Definition
children.detail: A Graft is a piece of tissue completely detached from its blood supply at the donor site and transferred to a recipient bed, from which it must acquire a new blood supply to survive.

children.title: Plasmatic Imbibition (0–48 hours)
children.detail: The graft absorbs nutrients and oxygen via passive diffusion from the plasma exudate of the recipient bed, held by a fibrin layer.

children.title: Inosculation (48–72 hours)
children.detail: Capillary buds from the recipient bed align and connect with existing cut vessels on the undersurface of the graft.

children.title: Neovascularisation / Revascularisation (Day 4–7)
children.detail: New blood vessels actively grow into the graft, establishing definitive circulation.

children.title: Haematoma or Seroma collection beneath the graft (prevents capillary contact during inosculation)
Shearing forces (disrupts fragile new capillary buds)
Infection: Specifically Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes
children.detail: Produces fibrinolysins/streptokinase that dissolve the fibrin attachment and destroy the entire graft.

children.title: Cannot support a skin graft and require a vascularised Flap
Comparison of Split-Thickness vs Full-Thickness Skin Grafts (Table surgery-tbl-003)
Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: Epidermis + a variable fraction of dermis (Thin: 0.15–0.3 mm; Intermediate; Thick: 0.45–0.6 mm).

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: Entire Epidermis + Entire Dermis (stripped clean of all subcutaneous fat).

children.title: Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: Thigh (anterolateral/medial), buttocks, back, abdominal wall.

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: Postauricular crease, supraclavicular fossa, upper eyelid, groin crease, flexor wrist crease.

children.title: Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: Heals spontaneously within 10–14 days by re-epithelialisation from residual dermal adnexa (pilosebaceous units/sweat glands).

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: Must be closed primarily with sutures (limits the size of graft that can be harvested).

children.title: Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: Reliable and rapid take (thin tissue has lower metabolic demand); can be meshed (1:1.5 to 1:6) to cover large areas and allow fluid drainage.

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: Slower, more precarious take (thick dermis increases diffusion distance); requires an pristine, well-vascularised bed.

children.title: Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: High Primary Contraction (minimal elastin recoil) is low, but Secondary Contraction (myofibroblast-mediated scar contraction during healing) is high.

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: High primary contraction (40% recoil on harvest), but minimal secondary contraction on the recipient bed.

children.title: Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: Poor colour/texture match, hairless, abnormal pigmentation, prone to contracture.

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: Excellent colour, texture, and elasticity match; retains hair follicles and sweat glands.

children.title: Split-Thickness Skin Graft (STSG / Thiersch Graft)
children.detail: Resurfacing large defects, acute burns, granulating ulcers, and flap donor sites.

children.title: Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG / Wolfe Graft)
children.detail: Face (nose, eyelids, lips), palmar surface of hand/digits (syndactyly release, burn contractures), and over mobile joints.

children.title: Harvested under local or general anaesthesia using a manual skin-grafting knife (Humby's knife, Watson's knife, or Silver's knife) or a powered Dermatome after lubricating the skin and blade with liquid paraffin

The graft is fenestrated/meshed, laid shiny-side (dermis) down on the debrided recipient bed, secured with absorbable sutures/staples or fibrin glue, and immobilised with a bolster (tie-over dressing) or Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy (VAC) for 5 days
The donor site is dressed with calcium alginate (Kaltostat) and left undisturbed for 10–14 days

children.title: Definition
children.detail: A block of tissue transferred from a donor site to a recipient defect while maintaining its own innate blood supply via a vascular pedicle (or re-established via microvascular anastomosis).

children.title: Covering avascular beds

children.title: Providing padding over pressure points (pressure sores)
The “Five Cs” Classification of Flaps (Bailey & Love)
Random Pattern Flaps
children.detail: Supplied by the subdermal vascular plexus without a named vessel; limited by length-to-breadth ratio, typically 1:1 to 2:1, up to 3:1 on the face.

children.title: Axial Pattern Flaps
children.detail: Contain a specific anatomically named artery and vein running along the long axis of the flap.

children.title: Forehead flap based on supratrochlear artery
Groin flap based on superficial circumflex iliac artery
Fasciocutaneous (Cormack & Lamberty Types A–D)
children.detail: e.g. Radial forearm flap.

children.title: Osseocutaneous
children.detail: Free fibula flap.

children.title: Regional (nearby)
children.detail: e.g. Pectoralis major flap to neck.

children.title: Distant
children.detail: Pedicled groin flap or Microvascular Free Flap such as Anterolateral Thigh [ALT] or DIEP flap.

children.title: Contour (Method of Movement for Local Flaps)
V-Y advancement
children.detail: e.g. fingertip amputation.

children.title: Conditioning
children.detail: Flap “delay”: surgical division of part of the blood supply 2 weeks prior to transfer to open choke vessels and augment axial survival.

children.title: Autologous Vein Grafts
children.detail: Gold standard for small/medium-calibre infrainguinal arterial bypasses (femoropopliteal, femorodistal, coronary, and traumatic vascular repair).

children.title: Reversed
children.detail: So venous valves do not obstruct arterial flow.

children.title: In situ

Synthetic Prosthetic Grafts

children.title: Dacron (woven or knitted polyethylene terephthalate)

children.title: Femoropopliteal bypass
children.detail: With a distal autologous vein collar — Miller cuff or St Mary's boot — to reduce intimal hyperplasia.

data.title: Q4.1: Premalignant Conditions of the Oral Cavity & Leukoplakia

children.title: Erythroplakia
children.detail: Bright red velvety plaque that cannot be characterised clinically or pathologically as any other condition; carries the highest risk of malignant transformation (>50% harbour severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ at biopsy).

children.title: Speckled Leukoplakia (Erythroleukoplakia)
children.detail: Mixed white nodular patches on an erythematous base; carries a much higher malignant risk than homogeneous leukoplakia.

children.title: Proliferative Verrucous Leukoplakia (PVL)
children.detail: Multifocal, exophytic, progressive white lesions in elderly women (often non-smokers) with a near 100% eventual malignant transformation rate.

children.title: Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF)
children.detail: Chronic, insidious progressive juxta-epithelial fibrosis of the oral mucosa caused by areca nut (betel quid / gutka) chewing; causes burning sensation, blanching of mucosa, palpable fibrous bands, and progressive trismus.

children.title: Oral Lichen Planus
children.detail: Especially the erosive / atrophic type; 1% risk.

children.title: WHO Definition
children.detail: A predominantly white patch or plaque of the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off and cannot be characterised clinically or pathologically as any other definable disease.

children.title: Spices / betel quid (areca nut + slaked lime)
Homogeneous
children.detail: Flat, thin, uniform white plaque with low malignant potential.

children.title: Non-homogeneous
children.detail: Nodular, verrucous, or speckled / erythroleukoplakia.

children.title: Factors Increasing Malignant Transformation Risk (Summary Box 53.2)
High-risk anatomical subsite
children.detail: Floor of mouth and ventral / lateral border of tongue.

children.title: Cessation of Risk Factors
children.detail: Stop tobacco, betel quid, and alcohol; smooth sharp teeth.

children.title: Incisional Biopsy
children.detail: Mandatory from the most indurated or red / speckled area to grade dysplasia (mild, moderate, severe) or rule out invasive SCC.

children.title: Mild dysplasia
children.detail: May be observed with serial photography and medical antioxidants (retinoids / lycopene).

children.title: Moderate-to-severe dysplasia
children.detail: Requires surgical excision (scalpel or CO_2 laser ablation) with lifelong surveillance.

data.title: Q4.2: Oral Cavity Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Carcinoma Tongue & Buccal Mucosa)

children.title: >95% of oral cavity cancers are Squamous Cell Carcinomas (OCSCC)
Western countries
children.detail: Lateral border of the tongue and floor of the mouth are the commonest sites.

children.title: India and South Asia
children.detail: Buccogingival sulcus and retromolar trigone account for >40% of cases (“alveolobuccal complex” cancer due to keeping smokeless tobacco / gutka / khaini quid in the gingivobuccal sulcus).

children.title: Betel quid (areca nut, catechu, slaked lime)
HPV-16/18
children.detail: Accounts for ~5% of oral cavity SCC vs 50–70% of oropharyngeal SCC.

children.title: Ulcerative (commonest)
children.detail: Hard indurated base with raised everted edges.

children.title: Verrucous carcinoma (Ackerman's tumour)
children.detail: Slow-growing, locally invasive, pushing margins, rarely metastasises.

children.title: Tongue
children.detail: Infiltrates intrinsic / extrinsic tongue muscles (causing ankyloglossia), floor of mouth, lingual / inferior alveolar nerves, and mandible (via direct erosive or infiltrative contact).

children.title: Buccal mucosa
children.detail: Invades buccinator, skin of cheek (resulting in an orocutaneous fistula), and pterygoid muscles (causing trismus).

children.title: Drains primarily to Levels I, II, and III
children.detail: Submental, submandibular, and upper / middle jugular nodes.

children.title: Tongue tip drains to Level IA
Lateral tongue drains to Levels IB and II
children.detail: Known propensity for “skip metastases” directly to Level III or IV and bilateral drainage if the lesion approaches / crosses the midline.

children.title: Severe local pain and referred ipsilateral otalgia
children.detail: Mediated via the lingual nerve → chorda tympani / mandibular nerve (V_3) → auriculotemporal nerve.

children.title: Excessive salivation, foetor oris, bleeding, and dysarthria (“hot potato speech”)
Ankyloglossia
children.detail: Fixation of the tongue to the floor of the mouth; tongue deviates to the ipsilateral side on protrusion.

children.title: Trismus
children.detail: Indicates invasion of the medial pterygoid muscle / masticator space.

children.title: Unexplained tooth mobility or palpable hard cervical lymphadenopathy
AJCC 8th Edition TNM Staging (Key Updates)
children.detail: Incorporates Depth of Invasion (DOI) (measured from the basement membrane of adjacent normal mucosa) into T-staging, and Extranodal Extension (ENE) into N-staging.

children.title: T1: Size ≤ 2 cm and DOI ≤ 5 mm
T2: Size ≤ 2 cm with DOI 5–10 mm; OR Size 2–4 cm with DOI ≤ 10 mm
T3: Size >4 cm OR any tumour with DOI >10 mm
T4a (Moderately advanced)
children.detail: Invades through cortical bone of mandible / maxilla, maxillary sinus, inferior alveolar nerve, deep / extrinsic muscles of tongue (genioglossus, hyoglossus, palatoglossus, styloglossus), or skin of face.

children.title: T4b (Very advanced / Unresectable)
children.detail: Invades masticator space, pterygoid plates, skull base, or encases the internal carotid artery.

children.title: Incisional / Wedge Biopsy
children.detail: From the growing edge of the ulcer (avoid central necrosis) for histopathological confirmation.

children.title: MRI with contrast
children.detail: Gold standard for defining soft-tissue extent, tongue muscle invasion, perineural spread, and marrow invasion.

children.title: Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT)
children.detail: Superior for assessing cortical bone invasion of the mandible / maxilla and staging the neck and thorax.

children.title: Orthopantomogram (OPG)
children.detail: Evaluates dental status prior to radiotherapy and gross mandibular erosion.

children.title: USG Neck + FNAC of suspicious cervical lymph nodes
Examination Under Anaesthesia (EUA) / Panendoscopy
children.detail: For posterior tumours and to rule out synchronous upper aerodigestive tract primaries (present in 2.5–4.5%).

children.title: Excision with a 1 cm circumferential clinical margin of normal tissue
Transoral approach for anterior T1/T2 lesions
Lip-split mandibulotomy for posterior oral cavity / tongue base lesions
Tongue Resection
children.detail: Partial glossectomy / hemiglossectomy / total glossectomy.

children.title: Tumour abuts periosteum without bone invasion
children.detail: Rim (Marginal) Mandibulectomy (preserving continuity of the lower border).

children.title: Gross medullary / cortical bone invasion present
children.detail: Segmental Mandibulectomy (or hemimandibulectomy).

children.title: Clinically Node-Negative (cN0) in T1/T2 tumours (especially DOI >3–4 mm)
children.detail: Prophylactic Elective Selective Neck Dissection (Supraomohyoid Neck Dissection: Levels I–III) (or I–IV for oral tongue) significantly improves overall and disease-free survival compared with “watch and wait” (Tata Memorial Hospital / D'Cruz et al. NEJM Trial). Sentinel lymph node biopsy is an alternative in select early T1 lesions.

children.title: Clinically Node-Positive (cN+)
children.detail: Therapeutic Modified Radical Neck Dissection (Levels I–V).

children.title: Small Defects
children.detail: Primary closure or local flaps (Facial Artery Myomucosal [FAMM] flap, nasolabial flap, buccal fat pad).

children.title: Moderate Soft-Tissue Defects (Partial Glossectomy / Buccal Mucosa)
children.detail: Radial Forearm Free Flap (RFFF) (thin, pliable, long pedicle).

children.title: Large / Subtotal Glossectomy Defects
children.detail: Anterolateral Thigh (ALT) Free Flap or pedicled Pectoralis Major Myocutaneous (PMMC) Flap (provides bulk to contact the palate for speech and swallowing).

children.title: Segmental Mandibular Defects
children.detail: Free Fibula Osseocutaneous Flap (gold standard; provides up to 25 cm of bone suitable for dental implants), Deep Circumflex Iliac Artery (DCIA), or Scapula free flap.

children.title: Adjuvant Radiotherapy (60–66 Gy)
children.detail: Indicated for T3/T4 primary, close margins (1–4.9 mm), multiple positive nodes, N2/N3 disease, Perineural Invasion (PNI), or Lymphovascular Invasion (LVI).

children.title: Concurrent Cisplatin-based Chemoradiotherapy
children.detail: Mandatory for Major High-Risk Features: Positive surgical margins (<1 mm) and/or Extranodal Extension (ENE).

data.title: Q4.3: Dentigerous Cyst & Differential Diagnosis of Tongue Ulcers

children.title: Definition
children.detail: A benign odontogenic cyst that surrounds the crown of an unerupted (impacted) permanent tooth, attached at the cementoenamel junction, arising from fluid accumulation between the reduced enamel epithelium and the tooth crown.

children.title: Second most common odontogenic cyst (after radicular / dental cyst); occurs in young adults (10–30 years)
Most commonly involves the mandibular third molar or maxillary permanent canine
Painless, slow-growing bony swelling expanding the outer cortical plate of the jaw
children.detail: Resulting in egg-shell crackling on palpation; with a missing permanent tooth in the dental arch.

children.title: Radiology (OPG)
children.detail: Well-defined unilocular radiolucency with a sclerotic margin enveloping the crown of an unerupted tooth, displacing the tooth towards the lower border of the mandible.

children.title: Potential transformation of the lining into an ameloblastoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Small cysts
children.detail: Complete surgical enucleation along with extraction of the unerupted tooth.

children.title: Large cysts
children.detail: In children or where enucleation risks jaw fracture / nerve injury: initial marsupialisation (decompression) to allow bone regeneration and tooth eruption, followed by delayed enucleation if necessary.

children.title: Dental ulcer
children.detail: Caused by a sharp jagged tooth or denture along the lateral border; heals within 2 weeks of removing the cause.

children.title: Aphthous ulcers
children.detail: Small, painful, recurrent, yellowish floor with erythematous halo.

children.title: Tuberculous Ulcer
children.detail: Painful, shallow, multiple ulcers at the tip / anterior margin with undermined edges.

children.title: Primary chancre (painless indurated ulcer at the tip)
Tertiary gummatous ulcer (deep punched-out painless ulcer on the midline dorsum)
Squamous cell carcinoma
children.detail: Painless non-healing ulcer >2 weeks with everted edges and indurated base.

data.title: Q5.1: Classification of Salivary Gland Tumours, Pleomorphic Adenoma & Parotidectomy

children.title: Covers: KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 17, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers
80% of salivary gland neoplasms arise in the major glands, and ~80% of these occur in the Parotid gland
80% of parotid tumours are benign, and 80% of benign parotid tumours are Pleomorphic Adenomas
Smaller the salivary gland, higher the likelihood of malignancy
2. WHO Classification of Salivary Gland Neoplasms (Table 54.3)
Warthin’s tumour (Adenolymphoma / Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum — second commonest benign tumour)
Low-grade Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (commonest salivary malignancy overall and in children)
Adenoid cystic carcinoma (propensity for perineural invasion and “Swiss-cheese” cribriform histology)
Non-Hodgkin’s MALT lymphoma (associated with Sjögren’s syndrome)
Peaks in the 3rd to 5th decades (average age 45 years)
>80% occur in the parotid (mostly in the superficial lobe / tail of parotid)
Well-circumscribed, firm, lobulated/bosselated mass with a whitish-tan, cartilaginous cut surface
Fibrous capsule is incomplete and has microscopic pseudopods (finger-like extensions) projecting into the surrounding normal gland parenchyma
It leaves behind pseudopods, leading to multifocal recurrence
Biphasic admixture of epithelial and myoepithelial cells (ducts, sheets, strands) embedded in a mesenchymal-like stroma (myxoid, mucoid, chondroid/cartilaginous, and hyalinised matrix)
Myoepithelial cells express p63, S-100, and SMA
Slow-growing, painless, firm-to-cartilaginous swelling in the parotid region (in front of and below the ear lobule, obliterating the retromandibular groove and lifting the ear lobule)
Freely mobile over deeper structures (becomes less mobile when the masseter is contracted)
Facial nerve is completely intact (0% palsy in benign lesions)
May pass through the stylomandibular tunnel (“dumbbell tumour”) to present as a medial paratonsillar / soft palate bulge pushing the tonsil medially
Clinical Features Suggestive of Malignant Transformation (Carcinoma ex Pleomorphic Adenoma)
Sudden rapid increase in size of a longstanding swelling
Shows a well-defined, lobulated hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic enhancement
Reported using the Milan System (Categories I–VI; Pleomorphic adenoma = Category IVA)
Core biopsy is reserved for inconclusive cases or suspected lymphoma
Open incisional biopsy is contraindicated due to tumour seeding
Indicated for large tumours (>4 cm), suspected deep lobe involvement, recurrent tumours, or suspected malignancy
Excision of the tumour with a cuff of normal surrounding parotid tissue while preserving the facial nerve
Superficial Parotidectomy (or Adequate Parotidectomy / Extracapsular Dissection in select mobile tail lesions)
For tumours lateral to the facial nerve plane (Patey’s faciovenous plane)
Excising both superficial and deep lobes while preserving the facial nerve
Sacrificing the facial nerve with immediate cable nerve grafting using the great auricular nerve or sural nerve, plus neck dissection and adjuvant radiotherapy
Lazy-S (Modified Blair) incision (preauricular crease, curving around the ear lobule over the mastoid, and running forward in a neck crease two finger-breadths below the angle of the mandible)
Raise an anterior skin flap in the subplatysmal / sub-SMAS plane
Divide the anterior branch of the great auricular nerve while preserving its posterior branch if possible
Anatomical Landmarks to Identify the Facial Nerve Trunk (Antegrade Technique)
Facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and 1 cm inferior to the cartilaginous tip of the tragus
Nerve lies just superior to the upper border of the posterior digastric near its mastoid insertion
Nerve lies 6–8 mm deep/inferior to the drop-off of this bony suture line (most constant landmark)
Nerve lies superficial to its base
Tracing peripheral branches — e.g., buccal branch parallel to Stensen’s duct or marginal mandibular branch crossing facial vessels — proximally to the trunk
Dissect in Patey’s faciovenous plane immediately superficial to the facial nerve branches using fine mosquito forceps and bipolar cautery up to Stensen’s duct, which is ligated
Place a suction drain and close in layers
Temporary facial nerve paresis (neuropraxia; commonest in the marginal mandibular branch)
Permanent facial nerve palsy (requires eye care to prevent exposure keratitis)
Numbness of the ear lobule (due to division of the great auricular nerve — C2, C3)

data.title: Q5.2: Warthin’s Tumour & Frey’s Syndrome

children.title: Second most common benign salivary gland tumour (5–15% of parotid neoplasms)
Occurs almost exclusively in the Parotid gland (typically in the lower pole / tail)
Strongly associated with cigarette smoking (8-fold higher risk)
Affects older men in their 6th to 7th decades (male:female historically predominance, now equalising with smoking trends)
10% are bilateral and 10% are multifocal (synchronous or metachronous)
Thought to arise from heterotopic salivary ductal inclusions trapped within intraparotid lymph nodes during late embryological encapsulation of the parotid
Cut surface shows cystic spaces filled with murky, chocolate-brown mucoid fluid (“motor-oil fluid”)

Papillary and cystic structures lined by a characteristic double layer of eosinophilic oncocytic epithelial cells (rich in mitochondria) resting on a dense reactive lymphoid stroma with germinal centres
On Technetium-99m ((99m)Tc) pertechnetate scintigraphy, Warthin’s tumour is uniquely “Hot” (concentrates radioisotope due to high mitochondrial content in oncocytic cells)

Following parotidectomy or parotid trauma, severed postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres undergo aberrant regeneration and cross-innervate the sympathetic-innervated dermal sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels of the overlying skin flap
Inferior salivatory nucleus → Glossopharyngeal nerve [CN IX] → Jacobson’s nerve → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve
Both parasympathetic secretomotor fibres and sympathetic fibres use acetylcholine as their neurotransmitter
Eating or thinking of food (salivary stimulus) triggers inappropriate sweating, flushing, erythema, and warmth over the preauricular/cheek skin in the distribution of the auriculotemporal nerve
Paint the affected preauricular skin with iodine solution, allow it to dry, dust with dry white starch powder, and give the patient a sialogogue (lemon slice)
Sweating dissolves the iodine to react with starch, turning the affected skin dark blue-black
Raise a thick skin flap (preserving SMAS)
Or interpose a physical barrier between the parotid bed and skin (e.g., sternocleidomastoid muscle flap, temporalis fascia flap, acellular dermal matrix [Alloderm], or autologous fat graft)
Management of Established Frey’s Syndrome (Summary Box 54.9)
Intradermal Botulinum Toxin A injections into the affected skin (gold standard)
Blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuroglandular junction
Tympanic Neurectomy (division of Jacobson’s nerve on the promontory of the middle ear) for refractory cases

data.title: Q5.3: Ranula, Submandibular Sialolithiasis & Stafne Bone Cyst

children.title: A mucous extravasation retention cyst of the floor of the mouth arising from rupture or obstruction of the ducts (ducts of Rivinus / Bartholin’s duct) or acini of the sublingual salivary gland

Presents in children/young adults as a unilateral, painless, soft, fluctuant, translucent bluish swelling in the anterior floor of the mouth lateral to the frenulum, resembling a frog’s belly (Latin: rana = frog)
The mucus collection herniates/insinuates through a dehiscence in the mylohyoid muscle (or around its posterior free border) into the submandibular/submental space
Presenting as a painless neck swelling with or without an intraoral component (bidigitally palpable)
MRI or USG confirms a cystic lesion with a “tail sign” extending into the sublingual space
Aspiration yields thick, viscid, mucinous saliva with high amylase (distinguishing it from a lymphatic malformation/cystic hygroma or dermoid cyst)
Excision of the ipsilateral Sublingual Gland along with decompression/evacuation of the cyst via a transoral approach (definitive cure)
Simple incision/drainage or marsupialisation has a high recurrence rate because the sublingual gland has multiple autonomous ducts
Non-surgical alternatives: Intralesional injection of sclerosant OK-432 (Picibanil) or Botulinum toxin
85% of all salivary calculi occur in the submandibular gland/Wharton’s duct (vs 15% in the parotid)
Submandibular secretion is rich in mucin, calcium, and phosphate, making it more viscous and alkaline
Wharton’s duct is long, tortuous, and has an antigravity ascending course with a narrow orifice (punctum), predisposing to salivary stasis
Acute, colicky pain and rapid tense swelling of the submandibular gland just before or during meals (especially sour foods)
Slowly subsides over 1–2 hours after eating
Reduced saliva from the inflamed sublingual papilla
Stone is palpable on bidigital palpation of the floor of the mouth (palpating from posterior to anterior)
80% of submandibular stones are radio-opaque (composed of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate)
High-Resolution Ultrasonography or non-contrast CT (detects radiolucent and small stones with acoustic shadowing)
Hydration, sialogogues, gland massage, and antibiotics if infected
Larger (>5 mm) impacted stones in the floor of the mouth: Transoral Choanal Duct Slitting (Sialolithotomy)
Place a stay suture behind the stone to prevent it from slipping back into the hilum
Incise the longitudinal axis of Wharton’s duct directly over the stone
Leave the duct open or marsupialise (never suture the duct closed as it causes stricture)
Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL for stones <7 mm)
Submandibular Gland Excision (preserving the marginal mandibular nerve, lingual nerve, and hypoglossal nerve)
3. Stafne Bone Cyst (Static Bone Cavity of Mandible) [KU 18]
A developmental pseudocystic depression on the lingual cortex of the mandible containing ectopic/entrapped submandibular salivary gland tissue and branches of the facial artery
A well-corticated, round, unilocular radiolucency (0.5–2 cm) located in the posterior mandible below the inferior alveolar nerve canal between the first molar and the angle of the mandible
Requires reassurance and no surgical intervention

data.title: Q6.1: Thyroglossal Cyst & Thyroglossal Fistula

children.title: The thyroid gland develops from the median endodermal bud at the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends caudally in front of the pharynx as the hollow thyroglossal duct
The duct passes in intimate continuity with (anterior, through, or posterior to) the body of the developing hyoid bone before reaching its final position in the lower neck
The duct normally obliterates by the 6th–8th week
Persistence of an unobliterated segment forms a Thyroglossal Cyst
Subhyoid / Infrahyoid (60–75% — Commonest): Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
Over the thyroid cartilage (often slightly to the left of the midline)
Floor of the mouth / Intralingual (Foramen caecum)
Presents most commonly in children and young adults as a painless, smooth, cystic midline neck swelling
Moves upwards on protrusion of the tongue (Tugging Sign)
Because the cyst remains tethered to the base of the tongue (foramen caecum) via the patent thyroglossal tract passing through the hyoid bone
Holding the cyst between thumb and index finger while asking the patient to protrude the tongue elicits a distinct upward tug
Recurrent Infection & Abscess Formation (due to lymphoid tissue in its wall)
Never congenital; always acquired following spontaneous rupture or inadequate surgical incision/drainage of an infected thyroglossal cyst
Presents as a midline pinpoint opening below the hyoid, discharging mucus/pus
Covered by a characteristic crescentic hood of skin (“hood sign”) superiorly that is pulled inwards on tongue protrusion
Almost always Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma arising in ectopic thyroid tissue within the cyst wall
Confirms the cystic nature of the swelling
Verifies the presence of a normal orthotopic thyroid gland in the lower neck (mandatory before excision, lest the cyst contains the patient’s only functioning thyroid tissue)
Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, Free T4) and FNAC (if a solid mural nodule is seen)
Excision of the cyst alone has a >40% recurrence rate because microscopic epithelial ductules pass through the hyoid bone up to the foramen caecum
Components of Sistrunk’s Operation: Complete en bloc excision of
The thyroglossal cyst (and fistulous tract with an ellipse of skin, if a fistula is present)
The central segment (body) of the hyoid bone (1–1.5 cm between the lesser cornua)
A core of suprahyoid muscle tissue (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, genioglossus) along the entire embryonic tract up to the foramen caecum

data.title: Q6.2: Solitary Thyroid Nodule (Discrete Thyroid Swelling) & Preoperative Evaluation

children.title: KU 24, 23, 20, 15, RGU, TU — Long Essay & Short Answers
Isolated (Solitary) Swelling — 70%
children.detail: A discrete palpable nodule in one lobe with an otherwise impalpable thyroid gland.

children.title: Dominant Swelling — 30%
children.detail: A prominent discrete nodule in a gland with clinical evidence of generalised abnormality / multinodularity elsewhere.

children.title: Differential Diagnosis (Causes) of a Solitary Thyroid Nodule
Dominant nodule of a Multinodular Goitre
children.detail: ~50% of clinically 'solitary' nodules reveal impalpable nodules on USG.

children.title: Thyroid Cyst
children.detail: Simple colloid cyst or haemorrhage into a necrotic nodule / adenoma.

children.title: Thyroid Malignancy — 15% in isolated nodules; 7.5% in dominant nodules
Focal Thyroiditis
children.detail: Hashimoto's or subacute de Quervain's thyroiditis.

children.title: Risk of Malignancy in Discrete Swellings ('Rule of 12' — Fig 55.13)
Isolated vs dominant nodules — risk twice as high in isolated
children.detail: Isolated nodules: 24% solid / 12% cystic; dominant nodules: 12% solid / 6% cystic.

children.title: Solid vs cystic nodules — risk twice as high in solid nodules
Sex — risk four times higher in males
children.detail: 48% in a solid isolated nodule in a man vs 12% in a woman.

children.title: Hoarseness of voice / vocal cord palsy (RLN invasion)
1. Thyroid Function Tests (Serum TSH, Free T3, Free T4)
If TSH is suppressed (hyperthyroid) — Radioisotope Uptake Scan
children.detail: Perform a Radioisotope Uptake Scan ((99m)Tc or ¹²³I) to differentiate a hyperfunctioning 'Hot' Autonomous Toxic Adenoma (with suppression of the contralateral lobe; malignancy risk <1–5%) from a cold nodule in Graves' disease.

children.title: Gold standard imaging
children.detail: Evaluates nodule size, composition (solid vs cystic), margins, and lymph nodes (Levels II–VI).

children.title: Grading
children.detail: Graded via U-Classification (U1–U5) or ACR TI-RADS (TR1–TR5).

children.title: Investigation of choice for all indeterminate / suspicious nodules
children.detail: Reported via the UK RCPath Thy Classification (Table 55.2) (or Bethesda System).

children.title: Thy1 / Thy1c: Non-diagnostic / Non-diagnostic cystic
children.detail: Repeat USG-guided FNAC.

children.title: Thy2: Non-neoplastic (Benign colloid nodule / thyroiditis)
children.detail: Reassure & observe (unless compressive).

children.title: Thy3 (Thy3a / Thy3f): Follicular neoplasm / atypia
children.detail: Diagnostic Hemithyroidectomy (Total lobectomy + isthmusectomy), because FNAC cannot distinguish benign Follicular Adenoma from Follicular Carcinoma (requires histological proof of capsular and/or vascular invasion).

children.title: Thy4: Suspicious of malignancy
children.detail: Diagnostic Hemithyroidectomy or Total Thyroidectomy.

children.title: Thy5: Diagnostic of malignancy (e.g. Papillary / Medullary carcinoma)
children.detail: Definitive thyroid cancer surgery.

children.title: Flexible Nasolaryngoscopy
children.detail: Mandatory preoperatively to document vocal cord mobility.

children.title: Serum Thyroid Autoantibodies (Anti-TPO, Anti-Tg)
children.detail: And Serum Calcitonin / CEA (if Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma is suspected).

children.title: Indications for Surgery in a Solitary Thyroid Nodule (Table 55.4)
Strong Clinical Suspicion
children.detail: Male sex, extremes of age, hard / fixed mass, RLN palsy, cervical lymphadenopathy, recurrent cyst after aspiration.

children.title: Toxic Adenoma
children.detail: Hemithyroidectomy is curative.

data.title: Q6.3: Multinodular Goitre (MNG) & Retrosternal Goitre

children.title: KU 24, 22, 19, 18, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers
1. Etiopathogenesis & Natural History of Simple Multinodular Goitre
Etiology
children.detail: Driven by chronic or fluctuating TSH stimulation (and local growth factors / immunoglobulins) in response to subnormal circulating thyroid hormone synthesis.

children.title: Iodine Deficiency (Endemic Goitre)
children.detail: Daily iodine requirement is 0.1–0.15 mg. Common in mountainous regions (Himalayas, Alps, Andes).

children.title: Dyshormonogenesis (Sporadic Goitre)
children.detail: Genetic enzyme defects in iodine trapping, organification, or coupling (e.g. Pendred syndrome).

children.title: Dietary & Drug Goitrogens
children.detail: Brassica vegetables (cabbage, kale, turnips contain thiocyanates that inhibit iodide trapping), Cassava, Lithium, Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), Carbimazole, and excessive iodides (Wolff–Chaikoff effect).

children.title: Physiological Increased Demand
children.detail: Puberty and pregnancy (Female:Male preponderance due to oestrogen receptors on thyrocytes).

children.title: 5-Stage Natural History of Simple Goitre (Bailey & Love)
Stage 1 — Diffuse Hyperplasia
children.detail: Persistent TSH stimulation causes uniform, diffuse follicular hyperplasia (Diffuse Hyperplastic Goitre — soft, smooth, reversible if TSH stimulus ceases).

children.title: Stage 2 — Fluctuating Stimulation
children.detail: Alternating periods of stimulation and involution produce mixed areas of active hyperplastic lobules and inactive colloid-filled lobules (Colloid Goitre).

children.title: Stage 3 — Focal Haemorrhage & Necrosis
children.detail: Active hyperplastic lobules outgrow their blood supply → central haemorrhage and necrosis, leaving a surrounding rim of active follicles.

children.title: Stage 4 — Nodule Formation
children.detail: Necrotic lobules coalesce to form discrete nodules filled with iodine-free colloid or inactive follicles, surrounded by fibrous tissue, cystic degeneration, and calcification.

children.title: Stage 5 — Multinodular Goitre (MNG)
children.detail: Continual repetition of this cycle produces an asymmetric, bosselated Multinodular Goitre, where most nodules are inactive and hormone synthesis occurs only in the internodular tissue.

children.title: Tracheal Compression & Displacement
children.detail: Lateral deviation or 'scabbard trachea' from retrosternal extension → dyspnoea and stridor (Kocher's test: slight lateral compression of the thyroid lobes elicits stridor).

children.title: Acute Airway Obstruction
children.detail: Sudden haemorrhage into a cyst / nodule impacted in the rigid thoracic inlet.

children.title: Secondary Thyrotoxicosis (Plummer's Disease)
children.detail: Develops in up to 30% of longstanding MNGs in middle-aged / elderly patients; hyperfunction occurs in internodular tissue or autonomous nodules; predominantly manifests with cardiovascular symptoms (atrial fibrillation, tachycardia, heart failure) without eye signs.

children.title: Malignant Transformation (<3–5%)
children.detail: Usually Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (or Papillary carcinoma) in endemic goitres.

children.title: Definition & Pathogenesis
children.detail: A goitre in which >50% of the thyroid mass lies below the plane of the thoracic inlet. Arises from the lower pole of a multinodular goitre being drawn downwards into the superior mediastinum by negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration, gravity, and swallowing. Blood supply remains strictly cervical (from the inferior thyroid arteries).

children.title: Often asymptomatic; when symptomatic
children.detail: Causes dyspnoea (worse at night or on lying flat), stridor, dysphagia, and a persistent cough.

children.title: Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Obstruction Syndrome
children.detail: Dilated non-pulsatile neck and chest wall veins, facial plethora, and Pemberton's Sign (raising both arms straight above the head for 1 minute corks the goitre into the narrow thoracic inlet, causing facial congestion, cyanosis, distended neck veins, and inspiratory stridor).

children.title: Examination
children.detail: Lower border of the thyroid swelling cannot be palpated ('cannot get below the swelling'), dullness to percussion over the manubrium, and tracheal deviation.

children.title: CT Scan of Neck & Thorax (Gold Standard)
children.detail: Defines the exact lower limit of extension (anterior vs posterior mediastinum), relationship to the aortic arch, and severity of tracheal compression.

children.title: Surgical Management of MNG & Retrosternal Goitre
Indications for Surgery
children.detail: Compressive symptoms, retrosternal extension with tracheal narrowing, secondary toxicity, suspicion of malignancy, or cosmetic deformity.

children.title: Choice of Operation
children.detail: Total Thyroidectomy (followed by lifelong levothyroxine replacement at 1.6 μg/kg/day) is the procedure of choice for bilateral MNG to eliminate recurrence and avoid hazardous reoperative surgery. For asymmetric MNG confined to one lobe, Total Hemithyroidectomy is appropriate. (Subtotal thyroidectomy and Dunhill's procedure [total lobectomy + contralateral subtotal lobectomy] are largely obsolete due to high recurrence rates).

children.title: Approach for Retrosternal Goitre — >95% via cervical collar incision
children.detail: More than 95% can be delivered and excised via a standard cervical collar incision (because the arterial supply is in the neck; ligate superior pole vessels and middle thyroid vein first, then use gentle digital mobilisation on the capsule to deliver the retrosternal component upwards).

children.title: Median Sternotomy (with cardiothoracic backup) — required in <5%
children.detail: Malignancy, recurrent goitre, posterior mediastinal extension below the aortic arch, or 'iceberg' goitres wider than the thoracic inlet.

data.title: Q6.4: Thyrotoxicosis & Graves’ Disease

children.title: KU 23, 22, 19, RGU, TU — Long Essay, Short Essays & Short Answers
Diffuse Toxic Goitre (Graves' Disease — Primary Thyrotoxicosis)
children.detail: Autoimmune disorder in young women (20–40 years); diffuse vascular goitre appearing simultaneously with hyperthyroidism; CNS overactivity + extrathyroidal manifestations (ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid acropachy).

children.title: Toxic Multinodular Goitre (Secondary Thyrotoxicosis / Plummer's Disease)
children.detail: Superimposition of hyperthyroidism on a pre-existing simple nodular goitre in patients >50 years; cardiovascular symptoms predominate (atrial fibrillation, high-output cardiac failure); eye signs are absent.

children.title: Solitary Toxic Adenoma (Autonomous Nodule)
children.detail: Single hyperfunctioning follicular adenoma producing T3/T4 autonomously, suppressing pituitary TSH and the rest of the thyroid gland.

children.title: Hydatidiform mole / Choriocarcinoma (hCG cross-reacts with TSH receptor)
Autoantibodies
children.detail: IgG autoantibodies (TSH Receptor Antibodies [TRAb / TSH-RAb / LATS]) bind to and stimulate TSH receptors on follicular cell membranes with a protracted action (16–24 hours vs 1.5–3 hours for normal TSH).

children.title: Histology
children.detail: Diffuse acinar hyperplasia and hypertrophy lined by tall columnar epithelium with papillary infoldings and pale, vacuolated colloid showing a characteristic peripheral 'scalloped' appearance.

children.title: Symptoms
children.detail: Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, excessive sweating, palpitations, dyspnoea on exertion, fine tremors, irritability / insomnia, proximal muscle weakness, diarrhoea, and oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea.

children.title: General
children.detail: Sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, wide pulse pressure (water-hammer pulse), warm moist palms, fine resting tremor of outstretched hands and protruding tongue.

children.title: Thyroid Gland
children.detail: Diffuse, smooth, symmetrically enlarged, soft-to-firm vascular goitre with a palpable thrill and audible systolic / continuous bruit (best heard at the upper pole, where the superior thyroid artery enters).

children.title: Graves' Ophthalmopathy
children.detail: Driven by autoimmune inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition in retro-orbital fat and extraocular muscles.

children.title: Dalrymple's sign (visible upper scleral rim above the cornea)
Von Graefe's sign (lid lag on downward gaze)
Joffroy's sign (absence of forehead wrinkling on looking up)
Ophthalmoplegia (Moebius' sign — failure of convergence)
children.detail: Earliest muscle affected is the inferior rectus limiting upward gaze.

children.title: Pretibial Myxoedema (Thyroid Dermopathy)
children.detail: Bilateral, symmetrical, non-pitting, violaceous / reddish plaque-like thickening of the skin over the shins and dorsum of the feet due to dermal mucopolysaccharide (hyaluronic acid) deposition; occurs only in Graves' disease.

children.title: Thyroid Function Tests (Table 55.1)
children.detail: Undetectable / Suppressed TSH (<0.01 mU/L) with elevated Free T4 and Free T3 (in T3-toxicosis, Free T4 is normal while Free T3 is high).

children.title: Autoantibodies
children.detail: Elevated TRAb (diagnostic of Graves' disease, >95% sensitive) and Anti-TPO antibodies.

children.title: Isotope Scan ((99m)Tc or ¹²³I)
children.detail: Shows diffuse homogeneous high uptake in Graves' disease, patchy hot / cold areas in Toxic MNG, and a single 'hot' nodule with complete suppression of the remaining gland in Toxic Adenoma.

children.title: Carbimazole
children.detail: 30–40 mg/day initially for 8–12 weeks until euthyroid, then titrated down to maintenance 5–15 mg/day or a 'Block and Replace' regimen adding Levothyroxine 100–150 μg/day for 12–18 months.

children.title: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
children.detail: Preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm as it also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 → T3.

children.title: Mechanism
children.detail: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase (TPO), blocking iodide oxidation and organification.

children.title: Disadvantages
children.detail: High relapse rate (>50%) upon stopping; cannot cure autonomous toxic nodules; 0.2% risk of Agranulocytosis (warn patient to stop drug immediately and check FBC if sore throat or fever develops).

children.title: β-Blockers (Propranolol 40 mg TDS)
children.detail: Rapidly controls adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety) and inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 → T3.

children.title: Action
children.detail: Destroys hyperfunctioning thyroid cells via β-particle emission over 6–12 weeks.

children.title: Indications
children.detail: Relapsed Graves' disease after ATDs, Toxic Adenoma, and elderly / frail patients.

children.title: Contraindications
children.detail: Pregnancy, lactation (absolute), young children, and active moderate-to-severe Graves' ophthalmopathy (can worsen eye disease unless covered with oral prednisolone).

children.title: Outcome
children.detail: Leads to eventual hypothyroidism in 80% of Graves' patients.

children.title: C. Surgery (Total Thyroidectomy; or Hemithyroidectomy for Solitary Toxic Adenoma)
Indications
children.detail: Large goitre with compressive symptoms, Toxic MNG, severe Graves' ophthalmopathy, relapsed Graves' disease in young women planning pregnancy, suspicion of coexisting malignancy, or drug intolerance / non-compliance.

children.title: Preoperative Preparation (Mandatory to prevent Thyrotoxic Crisis / Storm)
Render biochemically euthyroid with Carbimazole
children.detail: Until the evening before surgery.

children.title: β-Blockade (Propranolol 40 mg TDS)
children.detail: Continued for 7 days postoperatively (as half-life of circulating T4 is 7 days).

children.title: Lugol's Iodine (5% iodine + 10% potassium iodide; 10 drops TDS orally for 10 days prior to surgery)
children.detail: Reduces gland vascularity and friability (Plummer's effect) and transiently blocks hormone release (Wolff–Chaikoff effect).

children.title: Choice of Operation in Graves' Disease (Table 55.5)
children.detail: Total Thyroidectomy is preferred over subtotal thyroidectomy as it provides immediate cure with 0% risk of recurrent toxicity (trading for predictable lifelong thyroxine replacement).

data.title: Q6.5: Thyroid Malignancies (Papillary, Follicular, Medullary) & Complications of Thyroidectomy

children.title: KU 25, 21, 20, 18, 17, 16, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers
1. Classification & Relative Incidence of Primary Thyroid Malignancies (Table 55.6 & 55.7)
Derived from Follicular Epithelium (Differentiated Thyroid Cancer — DTC)
Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC) & Hürthle Cell Carcinoma: 10%
Derived from Follicular Epithelium (Poorly Differentiated / Undifferentiated)
Derived from Parafollicular C-Cells (Neuroectodermal / Ultimobranchial body)
Primary Thyroid Lymphoma (B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma arising in Hashimoto's thyroiditis): 2.5%
2. Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC) & Management of DTC with Nodal Metastasis (Long Essays KU 17, 18)
Etiology & Genetics
children.detail: Childhood neck irradiation (e.g. Chernobyl disaster), RET/PTC1 and RET/PTC3 rearrangements, and BRAF V600E mutations.

children.title: Often multifocal and non-encapsulated; cystic change is common
'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei
children.detail: Optically clear, ground-glass chromatin with nuclear grooves and intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions.

children.title: Psammoma bodies
children.detail: Concentric laminated calcified spherules.

children.title: Lymphatic Spread
children.detail: Strong propensity for cervical lymph node metastasis (central compartment Level VI [Delphian / pretracheal / paratracheal] and lateral jugular chain Levels II, III, IV, V). (Note: An isolated cystic lateral neck node metastasis from an occult <1 cm papillary microcarcinoma was historically misnamed 'Lateral Aberrant Thyroid').

children.title: Age (<55 years vs ≥ 55 years in AJCC 8th Ed.)
Management of Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC & FTC)
Low-Risk Unifocal Tumour (1–4 cm, cN0, no extrathyroidal extension)
children.detail: Thyroid Lobectomy + Isthmusectomy. (Tumours <1 cm [Papillary microcarcinoma] can be managed by lobectomy or active surveillance).

children.title: High-Risk Tumour (>4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, multifocal / bilateral, or Node-Positive [as in Long Essays KU 17/18])
children.detail: Total Thyroidectomy (removes all thyroid tissue to enable subsequent Radioiodine ablation and serum Thyroglobulin monitoring).

children.title: Clinically / Radiologically Node-Positive (cN1a / cN1b)
children.detail: Compartment-Oriented Therapeutic Neck Dissection (Central compartment Level VI clearance + Selective / Modified Radical Lateral Neck Dissection of Levels IIa, III, IV, and Vb, preserving the spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid). 'Berry-picking' of individual nodes is contraindicated.

children.title: Prophylactic Central Neck Dissection (Level VI)
children.detail: Reserved for high-risk T3/T4 tumours.

children.title: 3. Postoperative Radioiodine (¹³¹I) Ablation
children.detail: Given 4–6 weeks post-total thyroidectomy (stimulated by either thyroxine withdrawal or recombinant human TSH [Thyrogen] so TSH >30 mU/L) to ablate residual thyroid remnants and microscopic metastases.

children.title: 4. TSH Suppression Therapy
children.detail: High-dose Levothyroxine to suppress TSH below <0.1 mU/L in high-risk patients (since DTC cells are TSH-dependent).

children.title: 5. Follow-Up
children.detail: Serial Serum Thyroglobulin (Tg) (and anti-Tg antibodies) + Neck Ultrasonography every 6–12 months.

children.title: Origin
children.detail: Arises from parafollicular C-cells (neural crest origin via ultimobranchial body); does NOT concentrate radioiodine and is NOT TSH-dependent.

children.title: Clinical Forms
children.detail: 75–80% Sporadic (unilateral) and 20–25% Familial (autosomal dominant RET proto-oncogene mutation on Chromosome 10; multicentric and bilateral).

children.title: MEN 2A (Sipple's Syndrome)
children.detail: MTC (100%) + Phaeochromocytoma (50%) + Parathyroid hyperplasia (20%).

children.title: MEN 2B
children.detail: Aggressive early-onset MTC + Phaeochromocytoma + Mucosal neuromas + Marfanoid habitus.

children.title: Histology
children.detail: Sheets / nests ('cell balls') of spindle / polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma (formed from procalcitonin polypeptides; stains apple-green birefringence with Congo Red).

children.title: Secretions
children.detail: Secretes Calcitonin and Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA) (used for diagnosis and postoperative tumour marker surveillance), plus serotonin, prostaglandins, and VIP (causing flushing and secretory diarrhoea in 30%).

children.title: Preoperative checks
children.detail: Exclude Phaeochromocytoma first (check plasma / 24h urinary metanephrines before any neck surgery) and check serum calcium / PTH and RET germline mutation.

children.title: Surgery
children.detail: Total Thyroidectomy + Bilateral Central Compartment (Level VI) Neck Dissection (+ therapeutic lateral neck dissection if lateral nodes are involved).
