children.detail: Primary Major Amputation (revascularising a dead, paralysed limb causes fatal hyperkalaemia, acidosis, and myoglobinuric renal failure — Haimovici's myonephropathic metabolic syndrome).

children.title: Dead Limb
children.detail: Irreversible gangrene (atherosclerosis, diabetes, embolism, frostbite).

children.title: Deadly Limb
children.detail: Life-threatening wet gangrene, gas gangrene, spreading necrotising fasciitis, osteosarcoma, or massive crush injury.

children.title: Dead Loss (Nuisance) Limb
children.detail: Intractable rest pain with unreconstructable CLTI, severe unrecoverable trauma, or flail/paralysed/contracted limb.

children.title: Guillotine Amputation
children.detail: An emergency, rapid, circular open amputation where skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscles, and bone are divided at the exact same level and left completely unsutured to allow free drainage of pus and gas (indicated in fulminant gas gangrene or overwhelming wet diabetic foot sepsis; followed later by formal revision/higher definitive closure once sepsis resolves).

children.title: Below-Knee Amputation (Burgess Long Posterior Flap or Skew Flap)
children.detail: Preserves the knee joint (drastically reducing the energy expenditure of walking with a prosthesis); ideal tibial stump length is 10–12 cm below the tibial tuberosity (never <8 cm), with the fibula divided 2 cm shorter than the tibia and the anterior tibial crest bevelled at 45°.

children.title: Principle
children.detail: Ablation of the L2, L3, and L4 lumbar sympathetic ganglia abolishes sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone specifically to the cutaneous arterioles of the foot and lower leg (opening cutaneous arteriovenous shunts and increasing skin blood flow to aid healing of superficial ischaemic ulcers and relieve rest pain; it does NOT improve intermittent claudication because skeletal muscle vessels are regulated by local metabolites, not sympathetic nerves).

children.title: Indications
children.detail: Non-reconstructable distal small-vessel occlusive disease (Buerger's disease, severe Raynaud's phenomenon) with rest pain or minor superficial digital ulceration (where ABPI >0.3), plantar hyperhidrosis, and Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (causalgia).

children.title: Chemical Lumbar Sympathectomy (Preferred today)
children.detail: Percutaneous CT- or fluoroscopy-guided injection of 5 mL of 6–10% Phenol in water (or absolute alcohol) anterolateral to the L2–L4 vertebral bodies.

children.title: Surgical Lumbar Sympathectomy
children.detail: Extraperitoneal approach via a transverse flank incision (pushing the peritoneum and ureter medially to expose the sympathetic chain lying in the groove between the psoas major muscle and vertebral bodies; on the right it lies behind the IVC, on the left beside the aorta). Excision of L2, L3, and L4 ganglia (preserving the L1 ganglion bilaterally in young men to prevent retrograde ejaculation).

data.title: Q10.3: Aortic Aneurysm, False/Cirsoid Aneurysm, Arteriovenous Fistula & Raynaud's Syndrome

children.title: Covers: KU 24, 18, RGU, TU — Short Answers
Definition
children.detail: A permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta to ≥ 1.5 times its normal diameter (≥ 3.0 cm) involving all three layers of the arterial wall (True aneurysm). 95% are infrarenal and degenerative/atherosclerotic (associated with smoking, male sex [4:1], age >65 years, hypertension, and matrix metalloproteinase degradation of medial elastin).

children.title: Asymptomatic (75%)
children.detail: Discovered incidentally on imaging or as a painless expansile epigastric/umbilical pulsation (pulsates both anteriorly and laterally on bimanual palpation).

children.title: Symptomatic Non-Ruptured
children.detail: Back, flank, or abdominal pain (due to rapid sac expansion or an Inflammatory AAA with dense white retroperitoneal fibrosis), or trash foot (distal microembolisation of mural thrombus).

children.title: Ruptured AAA (Surgical Emergency; 80% overall mortality)
children.detail: Classic triad of sudden severe abdominal/lumbar back pain + hypotension/shock + pulsatile abdominal mass (80% rupture posterolaterally into the retroperitoneum, allowing a brief window of tamponade; 20% rupture anteriorly into the free peritoneal cavity).

children.title: Investigations
children.detail: Abdominal Ultrasonography (for screening men at age 65 and surveillance of small AAAs) and CT Angiography (CTA) (gold standard for planning open vs endovascular repair; defines neck length/angulation and iliac access).

children.title: Asymptomatic AAA <5.5 cm
children.detail: Best medical therapy (smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, BP control) + serial USG surveillance (annual if 3.0–4.4 cm; 3-monthly if 4.5–5.4 cm).

children.title: Indications for Elective Repair
children.detail: Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm in men (≥ 5.0 cm in women), rapid growth >1 cm/year, or any symptomatic aneurysm.

children.title: Open Surgical Inlay Repair
children.detail: Midline laparotomy → infrarenal aortic and iliac cross-clamping → longitudinal opening of the aneurysm sac → oversewing lumbar and IMA back-bleeding → suturing a tube or bifurcated Dacron graft end-to-end inside the sac → closing the native sac over the graft (to prevent aortoduodenal fistula).

children.title: Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR)
children.detail: Deployment of a modular stent-graft (Dacron/ePTFE supported by nitinol stents) via the femoral arteries to exclude the aneurysm sac (lower 30-day mortality than open repair, but requires lifelong surveillance for Endoleaks Types I–V — Table 61.3).

children.title: Management of Ruptured AAA (Summary Box 61.5)
children.detail: Permissive hypotension (restrict IV fluids to keep systolic BP 70–100 mmHg so as not to blow off the retroperitoneal clot), crossmatch blood, urgent CTA if stable, and immediate transfer to theatre for emergency EVAR or Open clamping & repair.

children.title: False Aneurysm (Pseudoaneurysm)
children.detail: A pulsating haematoma communicating with the arterial lumen through a breach in the arterial wall; its sac wall does not contain the three arterial layers (intima, media, adventitia) but is lined only by compressed perivascular fibrous tissue and organised laminated clot. Caused by penetrating trauma, arterial catheterisation (femoral artery puncture), or anastomotic disruption. Treated by USG-guided percutaneous thrombin injection (if <3 cm with a narrow neck) or open surgical evacuation and suture repair.

children.title: Cirsoid Aneurysm
children.detail: A congenital high-flow arteriovenous malformation (AVM) occurring most commonly in the subcutaneous tissue of the scalp (superficial temporal and occipital vessels). Presents as a warm, compressible, tortuous "bag of pulsating worms" beneath the scalp with a palpable thrill, continuous machinery bruit, headache, and risk of torrential haemorrhage on ulceration. Treated by preoperative superselective transcatheter arterial embolisation followed by complete surgical excision.

children.title: Definition & Causes
children.detail: An abnormal direct communication between a high-pressure artery and a low-pressure vein bypassing the capillary bed.

children.title: Congenital
children.detail: Cirsoid aneurysm, Parkes-Weber syndrome.

children.title: Traumatic
children.detail: Penetrating stab/gunshot injury or iatrogenic catheterisation.

children.title: Surgically Created (Therapeutic)
children.detail: Brescia–Cimino radiocephalic or brachiocephalic AV fistula for haemodialysis access in end-stage renal disease.

children.title: Local
children.detail: Veins become dilated, tortuous, and thick-walled ("arterialisation"); pulsatile mass with a palpable systolic–diastolic thrill and a continuous "machinery murmur" (Gibson's murmur); distal limb ischaemia ("steal syndrome") and venous hypertension/ulceration.

children.title: Systemic
children.detail: Decreased total peripheral resistance → increased venous return, tachycardia, wide pulse pressure, cardiomegaly, and high-output left ventricular failure.

children.title: Nicoladoni–Branham's Sign
children.detail: Digital compression of the feeding artery proximal to a large AVF causes an immediate reflex bradycardia and normalization of pulse pressure (as sudden elimination of the low-resistance shunt raises systemic arterial pressure, stimulating carotid sinus baroreceptors).

children.title: Management
children.detail: Duplex USG + DSA/CTA. Traumatic/congenital AVFs are treated by endovascular coil/glue embolisation, covered stent-graft placement across the arterial defect, or open surgical quadruple ligation/excision with arterial reconstruction (simple proximal arterial ligation alone is contraindicated as collateral steal causes distal gangrene).

children.title: 4. Raynaud's Disease vs Raynaud's Syndrome (Raynaud's Phenomenon) [KU 24, RGU, TU]
Definition
children.detail: Episodic vasospasm of the digital arteries and cutaneous arterioles of the hands (and feet) triggered by exposure to cold or emotional stress, producing a classic triphasic colour sequence.

children.title: Local Syncope (White / Blanching)
children.detail: Intense digital arteriolar spasm empties the capillary bed → digits turn dead-white, cold, and numb.

children.title: Local Asphyxia (Blue / Dusky Cyanosis)
children.detail: Sluggish accumulation of deoxygenated blood in paralysed dilated capillaries and venules → digits become swollen and bluish-purple.

children.title: Reactive Hyperaemia (Red / Engorgement)
children.detail: Relaxation of arteriolar spasm floods the dilated capillary bed with oxygenated blood → digits become bright red with throbbing pain and paraesthesia.

children.title: Raynaud's Disease (Primary / Idiopathic)
children.detail: Occurs in young women (15–30 years), bilateral and symmetrical, normal peripheral pulses, no underlying systemic disease, and almost never causes digital gangrene (only rare micronodular pulp scars).

children.title: Raynaud's Syndrome (Secondary)
children.detail: Secondary to connective tissue/autoimmune diseases (Systemic Sclerosis / CREST syndrome [90%], SLE, Rheumatoid arthritis), occupational vibrating tools ("Vibration White Finger"), Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (cervical rib), Buerger's disease, β-blockers/ergot, or cryoglobulinaemia. Often unilateral/asymmetric and frequently progresses to severe digital ischaemic ulceration, pulp necrosis, and gangrene.

children.title: Conservative
children.detail: Strict avoidance of cold (electrically heated mittens/gloves), absolute cessation of smoking, and stopping vibrating tools or β-blockers; treat underlying autoimmune disease.

children.title: Medical
children.detail: Oral Calcium Channel Blockers (Nifedipine 10–20 mg TDS or Amlodipine) (first-line vasodilator), topical nitrates, Sildenafil (PDE-5 inhibitor), or Intravenous Iloprost (prostacyclin analogue) infusion for severe digital ulceration/critical ischaemia.

children.title: Surgical
children.detail: Digital sympathectomy (periarterial adventitial stripping) or conservative amputation of demarcated necrotic fingertips (cervicodorsal sympathectomy provides only transient relief in Raynaud's and has largely been abandoned).

data.title: 1. Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue PYQs

children.title: Pathology
children.detail: Acquired benign vascular lesion sharing histological characteristics with capillary haemangiomas (not truly pyogenic or granulomatous).

children.title: Clinical Features
children.detail: Rapidly growing, small (0.5–1.5 cm), raised, pedunculated, soft bright-red nodular lesion following trivial trauma; shows superficial ulceration and bleeds profusely on slightest touch. Common on fingers, lips, face, and gingiva.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Excision with a minimal margin (or curettage with cauterisation of the feeding base to prevent recurrence).

children.title: Etiology
children.detail: Malignant proliferative tumour of vascular endothelial cells causally linked to Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8 / KSHV).

children.title: (i) Classic
children.detail: Elderly Ashkenazi Jewish/Mediterranean men.

children.title: (ii) Endemic
children.detail: African.

children.title: (iii) Iatrogenic
children.detail: Post-transplant immunosuppression.

children.title: (iv) Epidemic / AIDS-defining
children.detail: HIV infection.

children.title: Clinical Features & Treatment
children.detail: Starts as multifocal red-brown/violaceous indurated skin plaques on extremities or oral mucosa that become nodular and ulcerate. Treated with Antiretroviral therapy (HAART), local radiotherapy, intralesional vinblastine, or systemic liposomal doxorubicin.

children.title: Pathophysiology
children.detail: Chronic, relapsing inflammatory disease of apocrine sweat gland-bearing skin (axillae, groins, perineum, inframammary folds). Characterised by follicular occlusion, folliculitis, and secondary bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Propionibacterium acnes), culminating in painful deep abscesses, interconnected epithelialised sinus tracts, and bridged "rope-like" scarring.

children.title: Risk Factors
children.detail: Female:Male = 4:1; begins after puberty and improves at menopause; strongly associated with obesity, smoking, and androgen excess (Hurley Stages I, II, and III).

children.title: General
children.detail: Weight loss, smoking cessation, loose aerated clothing, antiseptic washes/tea-tree oil.

children.title: Medical
children.detail: Long-term oral tetracyclines (Doxycycline) or Clindamycin + Rifampicin, antiandrogens, retinoids, or biologics (Adalimumab).

children.title: Surgical (for severe/refractory disease)
children.detail: Radical wide excision of all affected apocrine-bearing skin and subcutaneous tissue followed by split-skin grafting or flap reconstruction to prevent contractures.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: An acute, sharply demarcated superficial bacterial infection of the upper dermis and superficial cutaneous lymphatics caused by Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes.

children.title: Clinical Features
children.detail: Usually follows a minor skin breach on the face (butterfly distribution) or lower limb. Presents with a fiery-red, hot, oedematous, indurated plaque with a raised, palpable, sharply advancing margin (Milian's ear sign: involves the pinna, which lacks deeper subcutaneous tissue, unlike cellulitis), accompanied by high fever, rigors, and leukocytosis.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Swab any portal of entry; prompt oral or IV Penicillin (Benzylpenicillin / Amoxicillin) or macrolide.

children.title: Genetics & Pathophysiology
children.detail: Rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective nucleotide excision repair (NER) of UV-induced DNA pyrimidine dimers.

children.title: Clinical Features
children.detail: Extreme photosensitivity from infancy, severe freckling, xerosis, poikiloderma, ocular photophobia/keratitis, premature skin ageing, and a >2000-fold increased risk of multiple cutaneous malignancies (BCC, SCC, and Malignant Melanoma) appearing before age 10.

children.title: Prognosis & Management
children.detail: 60% mortality by age 20 from metastatic skin cancer. Managed by total UV avoidance, protective clothing/sunscreens, oral retinoids, and early excision of skin tumours.

children.title: Pathology
children.detail: Locally invasive, non-metastasising fibroblastic proliferation arising from musculoaponeurotic structures. Histologically benign (spindle cells in abundant collagen without atypia) but locally malignant due to infiltrative margins and high local recurrence.

children.title: Etiology
children.detail: Associated with pregnancy, prior surgical scars/trauma, oestrogen exposure, and Gardner's Syndrome / Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (APC gene mutation on Chr 5q22).

children.title: Sites
children.detail: Abdominal wall (especially infraumbilical rectus sheath in multiparous women), intra-abdominal (mesenteric fibromatosis in FAP), and extra-abdominal (shoulder girdle/pelvis).

children.title: Management
children.detail: Active surveillance first, medical therapy (NSAIDs [Sulindac], Tamoxifen, Sorafenib/Imatinib, or low-dose chemotherapy), or wide local excision with mesh reconstruction if symptomatic/progressive.

children.title: Pathology
children.detail: A bilocular cold abscess arising from caseating tuberculous lymphadenitis (typically in the jugulodigastric or posterior triangle nodes of the neck).

children.title: Mechanism
children.detail: Caseous pus is initially confined beneath the investing layer of deep cervical fascia (forming the deep loculus). Over time, it erodes through a small pinpoint perforation in the deep fascia to form a second fluctuating collection in the superficial subcutaneous space just beneath the skin (the superficial loculus), connected by a narrow track resembling a collar-stud.

children.title: Management
children.detail: 6–9 months of Anti-Tuberculous Therapy (ATT) + non-dependent zygomatic/oblique aspiration (or incision, curettage of both superficial and deep cavities, enlarging the fascial defect, and primary watertight closure without a drain to prevent a chronic tuberculous sinus).

data.title: 2. Oral Cavity PYQs

children.title: Cleft Lip & Palate (Types & Timing of Repair) [RGU, TU]
Embryology
children.detail: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the frontonasal (median nasal) process with the maxillary processes during the 5th–6th week of gestation. Cleft palate results from failure of fusion of the palatal shelves of the maxillary processes during the 7th–10th week.

children.title: Cleft Lip
children.detail: Unilateral (Left > Right; Incomplete vs Complete extending into the nostril floor and alveolus up to the incisive foramen [primary palate]) or Bilateral (with a protruding premaxilla/prolabium).

children.title: Cleft Palate
children.detail: Complete or Incomplete (bifid uvula, submucous cleft palate, soft palate only, or hard + soft palate [secondary palate]).

children.title: Cleft Lip Repair
children.detail: Performed at 3 to 6 months of age following Millard's "Rule of 10s" (Weight >10 lbs [4.5 kg], Age >10 weeks, Haemoglobin >10 g/dL, and WBC <10,000/mm³). Technique: Millard's Rotation–Advancement Repair (or Tennison–Randall triangular flap).

children.title: Cleft Palate Repair (Palatoplasty)
children.detail: Performed at 9 to 12 months of age (before speech development begins, while allowing early maxillary growth). Technique: Von Langenbeck bipedicled mucoperiosteal flap, Wardill–Kilner–Veau V-Y pushback, or Furlow's double-opposing Z-plasty.

children.title: Secondary Alveolar Bone Grafting
children.detail: Using cancellous iliac crest bone at 8–10 years (prior to permanent canine eruption).

children.title: Who it affects
children.detail: An acute, fulminating, gangrenous infective stomatitis affecting severely malnourished, debilitated children (often following measles, malaria, or gastroenteritis) in low-income regions.

children.title: Cause & Course
children.detail: Caused by a synergistic polymicrobial infection of Fusobacterium necrophorum, Borrelia vincentii, and anaerobes. Begins as a gingival ulcer that rapidly necroses through the full thickness of the cheek and jaws, sloughing off soft tissue and bone to leave grotesque facial defects and severe trismus.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Urgent fluid/nutritional resuscitation, IV Penicillin + Metronidazole, wound debridement, and delayed free/pedicled flap reconstruction.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Congenital anomaly characterised by an abnormally short, thick, fibrotic lingual frenulum tethering the ventral tip of the tongue to the floor of the mouth.

children.title: Clinical Features
children.detail: Infant cannot protrude the tongue tip beyond the lower incisors; on attempted protrusion, the tip is pulled down, creating a heart-shaped (notched) tongue; causes maternal nipple pain/difficulty latching during breastfeeding and later impairs pronunciation of lingual consonants (d, l, n, r, t, th).

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Simple division (Frenotomy) in infants with breastfeeding difficulty, or formal Frenuloplasty (horizontal division under general anaesthesia with vertical closure or Z-plasty) after age 1–2 years if speech is impaired.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Any benign localised swelling arising from the gingiva (gums) or periodontal membrane (Greek: epi = upon, oulon = gum).

children.title: Fibrous Epulis (Commonest)
children.detail: Firm, pink, pedunculated fibroma arising from the interdental papilla due to chronic irritation/calculus.

children.title: Granulomatous (Pyogenic / Pregnancy) Epulis
children.detail: Soft, bright-red, vascular gingival mass that bleeds easily; Pregnancy epulis appears in the 1st/2nd trimester due to hormonal gingivitis and regresses postpartum.

children.title: Giant Cell (Myeloid) Epulis (Peripheral Giant Cell Granuloma)
children.detail: Dark-red/plum-coloured vascular sessile swelling arising from the periosteum/periodontal ligament containing multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells (always check serum calcium/PTH to exclude a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism).

children.title: Carcinomatous Epulis
children.detail: Squamous cell carcinoma of the gingiva/alveolus.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Excision of the epulis along with curettage of its periosteal base and extraction of any involved/irritating tooth root.

children.title: Dental Cyst (Radicular / Periapical Cyst) vs Dental Abscess [TU]
Dental (Radicular) Cyst
children.detail: Commonest odontogenic cyst. Arises from epithelial cell rests of Malassez in the periodontal ligament stimulated by chronic periapical inflammation beneath a non-vital, carious, dead permanent tooth. Forms a slow-growing, painless jaw swelling lined by stratified squamous epithelium; OPG shows a round radiolucency with a sclerotic rim at the root apex of a carious tooth. Treated by endodontic root canal/tooth extraction + enucleation of the cyst.

children.title: Acute Dental (Alveolar) Abscess
children.detail: Suppurative infection of the dental pulp and periapical tissues tracking through cortical bone; presents with severe throbbing toothache (exacerbated by hot/cold and percussion), fever, trismus, and brawny swelling of the cheek/floor of mouth (Ludwig's angina if bilateral submandibular/sublingual spaces are involved). Treated with antibiotics (Amoxicillin + Metronidazole), drainage (via root canal, tooth extraction, or intraoral incision), and airway protection.

data.title: 3. Vascular PYQs

children.title: Definition
children.detail: A retroperitoneal high ligation of the testicular (internal spermatic) vessels performed for symptomatic varicocele or male infertility.

children.title: Incision
children.detail: A 3–4 cm transverse muscle-splitting incision made slightly above and medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (at the level of the deep inguinal ring).

children.title: Exposure
children.detail: The peritoneum is swept medially to expose the testicular veins (and testicular artery) on the psoas major muscle proximal to the internal ring, where the pampiniform plexus has coalesced into only 1 or 2 trunks.

children.title: Ligation en masse
children.detail: Vessels are ligated and divided en masse; testicular viability is maintained via the artery to the vas deferens and cremasteric artery.

children.title: Current practice
children.detail: Today, it is commonly performed laparoscopically, though subinguinal microsurgical varicocelectomy has lower hydrocele and recurrence rates.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: A classic radiological sign seen on Plain Chest X-ray (and Barium Swallow) in Coarctation of the Aorta.

children.title: Above
children.detail: Pre-stenotic dilatation of the aortic arch and left subclavian artery.

children.title: Middle
children.detail: Inward indentation of the coarctation waist.

children.title: Below
children.detail: Post-stenotic dilatation of the descending aorta.

children.title: Mirror-image “Reverse 3” (or “E”) sign
children.detail: The aortic contour indents the oesophagus in the opposite direction, producing a mirror-image “Reverse 3” (or “E”) sign.

children.title: Associated sign — Roesler's sign
children.detail: Inferior rib notching of ribs 3 to 9, caused by dilated tortuous posterior intercostal collaterals.

children.detail: Site of active mitosis/differentiation.

children.detail: Delicate collagen/elastin, dermal papillae, capillary/lymphatic plexuses, Meissner's corpuscles.

children.title: (2) Deep Reticular Dermis

Type I

children.title: Type V

children.detail: Retrograde collateral blood flow into the aneurysm sac from aortic branches (Inferior mesenteric artery or lumbar arteries).

children.detail: Structural failure of the stent-graft due to modular component disconnection (Type IIIa) or fabric tear/defect (Type IIIb).

data.title: 1. Chapter 45: Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Dimensions
children.detail: Surface area is 1–2 m², weight 15–20 kg. Epidermis is thickest on the sole of the foot (0.5–1 mm) and thinnest on the eyelid (0.05–0.09 mm).

children.title: Angiosomes (Taylor & Palmer)
children.detail: 3D composite blocks of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and underlying muscle/bone supplied by a specific named source artery and vein.

children.title: Choke vessels
children.detail: Neighbouring angiosomes are linked within muscle bellies by reduced-calibre “choke vessels” (which dilate during surgical flap delay or myocutaneous flap harvest, e.g., Latissimus dorsi and Rectus abdominis flaps).

children.title: Inheritance
children.detail: 70% autosomal dominant, 30% sporadic.

children.title: NF-1 (Von Recklinghausen's disease — Chr 17, 1:4000 births)
children.detail: ≥ 6 smooth-bordered (“Coast of California”) café-au-lait spots, cutaneous/subcutaneous neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign), iris Lisch nodules, and optic gliomas.

children.title: NF-2 (Chr 22)
children.detail: Bilateral acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) and CNS tumours.

children.title: Gorlin's Syndrome (Naevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome)
children.detail: Autosomal dominant mutation in the PTCH1 (“patched”) tumour suppressor gene on Chromosome 9q22–31. 90% develop multiple BCCs at an early age, palmar/plantar pits, odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw, calcified falx cerebri, bifid ribs, macrocephaly, hypertelorism, and medulloblastoma.

children.title: Ferguson-Smith Syndrome
children.detail: Rare autosomal dominant mutation on Chromosome 9q causing multiple self-healing squamous cell carcinomas unrelated to sun exposure.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Excessive eccrine sweating of palms, soles, axillae, and groins.

children.title: Stepwise treatment
children.detail: Topical 20% aluminium chloride antiperspirants, iontophoresis, intradermal Botulinum toxin A injections, or Endoscopic Transthoracic Sympathectomy (ETS) (T2–T3 ganglia for palmar/axillary hyperhidrosis).

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Localised or generalised loss of subcutaneous fat (complicating insulin injection sites, HIV protease inhibitors, or transplant drugs).

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Autologous fat grafting (lipotransfer) or poly-L-lactic acid fillers.

children.title: Presentation
children.detail: Rapidly enlarging, very painful necrotic cutaneous ulcer with a characteristic violaceous/purple undermined edge and cribriform scar.

children.title: Mechanism
children.detail: Mediated by neutrophil dysfunction (pathergy phenomenon).

children.title: Associations (50%)
children.detail: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Ulcerative colitis/Crohn's), Rheumatoid arthritis, Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, or Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Medical (high-dose systemic corticosteroids / cyclosporine / infliximab); surgical debridement is contraindicated as pathergy worsens ulceration.

children.title: Organisms
children.detail: Polymicrobial synergistic infection (Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus + S. aureus, E. coli, Pseudomonas, Bacteroides, Clostridium).

children.title: Spread
children.detail: Spreading rapidly along the deep fascial planes while initially sparing overlying skin.

children.title: Epidemiology
children.detail: 80% follow minor trauma/skin breach; 60% occur in lower limbs.

children.title: Variants
children.detail: Perineal variant = Fournier's gangrene; abdominal wall postoperative variant = Meleney's synergistic gangrene.

children.title: Severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs
Skin anaesthesia (thrombosis of perforating nutrient vessels and nerves)
Management
children.detail: Immediate fluid resuscitation + high-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Beta-lactam + Clindamycin + Metronidazole) + emergency radical surgical debridement back to healthy bleeding tissue, followed by relook debridement at 24 hours, VAC dressings, and split-skin grafting.

children.title: Cause
children.detail: Acute infectious (Neisseria meningitidis meningococcaemia or varicella in children <7 years or asplenia), neonatal, or idiopathic intravascular thrombosis mediated by endotoxin-induced Protein C deficiency.

children.title: Features & outcome
children.detail: Causes a petechial rash that coalesces into ecchymoses, haemorrhagic bullae, and sharply demarcated black gangrenous eschars, DIC, and multiorgan failure (40–50% mortality; often requires limb amputations).

children.title: Milia
children.detail: Tiny 1–2 mm hard white subepidermal keratin retention cysts seen in neonates and on chronic sun-damaged/smoker's facial skin in the elderly (Favre–Racouchot syndrome).

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Benign hamartoma arising from the neuromyoarterial glomus body (Sucquet–Hoyer arteriovenous shunt canal) responsible for thermoregulation, located most commonly in the subungual corium of the nail bed.

children.title: (2) Exquisite pinpoint tenderness (elicited with a pinhead — Love's sign, abolished by inflating a tourniquet — Hildreth's sign)
Treatment
children.detail: Subungual surgical excision.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Rare, highly aggressive primary neuroendocrine (mechanoreceptor) carcinoma of the skin in elderly white patients (women > men, 4:1; associated with Merkel cell polyomavirus and UVR).

children.title: Presentation
children.detail: Rapidly growing, painless, firm, red-purple dome-shaped nodule on sun-exposed head/neck.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Wide local excision (2.5–3.0 cm margin), SLNB, and adjuvant radiotherapy.

children.title: Congenital Wounds, Pressure Sores, Sinus & Fistula
Cutis Aplasia Congenita
children.detail: Congenital absence of epidermis, dermis (and underlying skull bone in 20%) at the vertex of the scalp.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Unilateral self-limiting atrophy of facial skin, subcutaneous fat, muscle, and bone (linear scleroderma variant; cranial forehead cleft variant is called en coup de sabre).

children.title: Reconstruction
children.detail: Reconstructed after burnout (5–10 years) using Coleman autologous lipotransfer or free flaps.

children.title: Definition
children.detail: Cone-shaped ischaemic necrosis over bony prominences (sacrum, ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, heel) when external tissue pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure (>32 mmHg); muscle and fat are more susceptible to ischaemia than skin (“iceberg” cone shape).

children.title: Management
children.detail: Pressure-relieving mattresses, 2-hourly turning, nutrition, VAC therapy, and surgical debridement + musculocutaneous flap reconstruction (e.g., Gluteus maximus or Tensor fascia lata flap).

children.title: Sinus
children.detail: A blind-ending granulation-lined tract connecting a deep cavity to an epithelial surface.

children.title: Fistula
children.detail: An abnormal communication connecting two epithelialised surfaces.

children.title: Causes of Persistence of a Sinus/Fistula
(1) Presence of a foreign body or necrotic tissue (suture, hair, bone sequestrum)

data.title: 2. Chapter 46: Burns (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Admission Referral Criteria to a Specialist Burns Unit (Table 46.1)
Any burn likely to require fluid resuscitation (>15% TBSA in adults, >10% TBSA in children)
Any deep burn likely to require surgical excision and grafting
Burns of any significance to special anatomical areas: Face, Hands, Feet, Perineum/Genitalia, or across major joints
Circumferential burns of limbs or chest
Burns at the extremes of age or with significant medical/psychiatric comorbidities
Any suspicion of Non-Accidental Injury (NAI)
children.detail: Delayed presentation, inconsistent history, symmetrical “glove and stocking” forced-immersion scalds with sharp water-line sparing flexion creases, or doughnut-shaped buttock sparing.

children.title: High-tension electrical burns, chemical burns (especially hydrofluoric acid), or ionising radiation burns
Acute Industrial Cold Injury vs Frostbite
children.detail: Acute Industrial Cold Injury (liquid nitrogen / LPG contact) vs Frostbite (freezing of extremities with intracellular ice crystal formation and microvascular stasis/thrombosis).

children.title: Rewarming
children.detail: Rapid rewarming in a circulating water bath at 40–42°C for 15–30 minutes (never use dry heat or rub the tissue).

children.title: Supportive care
children.detail: Analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis.

children.title: Wound care
children.detail: Strictly conservative wound care for 1–3 months until complete dry mummification and absolute demarcation occur (“Frostbite in January, amputate in July”), unless wet gangrene/sepsis supervenes.

children.title: Localised high-dose radiation
children.detail: Causes endarteritis obliterans and chronic painful radionecrotic ulcers that cannot support a skin graft and require wide excision + vascularised free flap cover.

children.title: Whole-body radiation
children.detail: Acute skin desquamation indicates a lethal dose.

data.title: 3. Chapter 47: Plastic & Reconstructive Surgery (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Principle
children.detail: A deflated silicone balloon expander is placed subcutaneously adjacent to a defect and serially inflated weekly with normal saline via a filling port. Overlying skin expands via mechanical creep (collagen fibre realignment and expulsion of interstitial water) and biological creep / stress relaxation (mitotic epidermal proliferation and dermal angiogenesis), surrounded by a vascular fibrous capsule.

children.title: Advantages & Indications
children.detail: Provides sensate skin of identical colour, texture, and hair-bearing quality without a distant donor defect. Ideal for scalp reconstruction (only way to create new hair-bearing scalp), giant congenital melanocytic naevi, burn scar contractures, and two-stage breast reconstruction.

children.title: Three steps
children.detail: (1) Low-pressure tumescent liposuction harvest (from abdomen/thigh), (2) Centrifugation (3000 rpm for 3 minutes) to separate oil and blood from viable adipocytes and adipose-derived stromal stem cells, and (3) Micro-droplet reinjection via blunt cannulae into multiple tissue planes (e.g., breast reconstruction contour defects, irradiated scars, Parry–Romberg syndrome). ~20–50% of grafted fat resorbs; rare risk of intravascular fat embolism.

children.title: Microsurgery, Free Flap Monitoring & Medicinal Leech Therapy
Free Flap Monitoring
children.detail: Keep the patient “Warm, Wet (hyperdynamic normovolaemia), and Comfortable (pain-free to prevent catecholamine-induced vasospasm)”. Monitor hourly in the first 48 hours for colour, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, handheld/implantable Doppler signal, and pinprick bleeding:

children.title: Arterial Thrombosis (1/3 of failures)
children.detail: Flap is pale/white, cool, flaccid/empty, absent capillary refill, and no bleeding on pinprick.

children.title: Venous Thrombosis/Congestion (2/3 of failures)
children.detail: Flap is dark purple/dusky blue, tense/swollen, very brisk capillary refill (<1 s), and rapid dark venous oozing on pinprick.

children.title: Action
children.detail: Release tight dressings/sutures at bedside and return immediately to theatre for microvascular exploration and revision anastomosis (>60% salvage rate if explored early).

children.title: Indication
children.detail: Salvage of venously congested flaps or distal digital/ear replants where venous outflow is insufficient or no suitable vein exists for microvascular anastomosis (never used for arterial insufficiency or main-pedicle venous thrombosis that can be surgically revised).

children.title: Mechanism
children.detail: Leech saliva contains hirudin (potent direct thrombin inhibitor), hyaluronidase, and histamine-like vasodilators; each leech ingests 5 mL of blood and the bite oozes up to 50–150 mL over several hours while neovascular venous channels grow in (takes 7–14 days).

children.title: Mandatory Prophylaxis
children.detail: The leech gut harbours the symbiotic Gram-negative bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila, which causes severe flap infection/necrosis; all patients must receive prophylactic Ciprofloxacin (quinolone) or Co-trimoxazole during leech therapy and regular haemoglobin monitoring.

data.title: 4. Chapter 53: Oral Cavity Cancer (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) in Early Oral Cancer

Used in cT1–T2 N0 oral cavity SCC as an alternative to upfront elective neck dissection. Peritumoral injection of (99m)Tc-nanocolloid + ICG/blue dye identifies the first draining node(s) (including unexpected contralateral drainage); if positive on step-serial sectioning and immunohistochemistry, completion neck dissection is performed.
Access Procedures for Oral Cancer Resection
Transoral Resection
children.detail: For anterior T1/T2 lesions.

children.title: Lip-Split Mandibulotomy
children.detail: Paramedian stepped osteotomy in front of the mental foramen (preserving the inferior alveolar nerve) to swing the hemimandible laterally for posterior tongue/oropharyngeal tumours.

children.title: Visor Flap / Mandibular Lingual Release (“Drop-down” approach)
children.detail: Subplatysmal apron incision releasing floor-of-mouth muscles from the inner mandible to drop the tongue into the neck without splitting the lip or bone.

children.title: Weber–Fergusson Incision
children.detail: Divides upper lip philtrum, curves around the ala and lateral nasal wall, and extends infraorbitally to expose the maxilla for Maxillectomy.

children.title: Virtual Surgical Planning (VSP), Zygomatic Implants & Immunotherapy
VSP
children.detail: Preoperative 3D CT CAD/CAM stereolithographic models and custom 3D-printed cutting guides for precise mandibular resection and fibula/scapula osteotomies.

children.title: ZIP (Zygomatic Implant Perforator) Flap
children.detail: Immediate placement of long zygomatic dental implants perforating through a radial forearm/ALT soft-tissue free flap to provide immediate fixed dental rehabilitation after maxillectomy without needing a bony free flap.

children.title: Immunotherapy in Recurrent/Metastatic HNSCC
children.detail: Anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (Pembrolizumab, Nivolumab) prolong overall survival in platinum-refractory or PD-L1-positive recurrent/metastatic oral SCC.

data.title: 5. Chapter 54: Disorders of the Salivary Glands (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Mucoceles, Necrotising Sialometaplasia & Immunological Salivary Disorders
Extravasation Mucocele
children.detail: Traumatic rupture of a minor salivary gland duct on the lower lip in children/young adults, spilling mucin into connective tissue (lacks an epithelial lining); presents as a painless, translucent bluish submucosal nodule; treated by surgical excision with the underlying minor salivary gland.

children.title: Acute Necrotising Sialometaplasia
children.detail: Self-limiting ischaemic infarction of minor salivary glands on the hard palate (triggered by local anaesthetic injection, trauma, or bulimia). Presents as a deep crateriform palatal ulcer with rolled margins that clinically and histologically mimics squamous cell carcinoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma (squamous metaplasia of ducts, but lobular architecture is preserved). Heals spontaneously within 6–10 weeks without surgery.

children.title: Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic destruction of exocrine glands (Female:Male = 10:1, age 40–60).
Primary SjS (Sicca Syndrome)
children.detail: Xerostomia (dry mouth) + Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) with bilateral parotid enlargement, without an associated connective tissue disease.

children.title: Secondary SjS
children.detail: Sicca symptoms + Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, or Scleroderma.

children.title: Diagnosis
children.detail: Anti-SSA (Ro) and Anti-SSB (La) antibodies, Rheumatoid factor, Schirmer’s test, and Labial Minor Salivary Gland Biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (Focus score ≥ 1 [≥ 50 lymphocytes per 4 mm²]).

children.title: Complication
children.detail: 40-fold increased risk of parotid MALT B-cell Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (suspect if a parotid gland enlarges rapidly or becomes hard).

children.title: Sarcoidosis & Heerfordt’s Syndrome
children.detail: Non-caseating granulomatous infiltration of the parotid gland; Heerfordt’s Syndrome (Uveoparotid Fever) is the classic triad of bilateral parotid enlargement + anterior uveitis + facial nerve (CN VII) palsy accompanied by low-grade fever.

children.title: HIV-Associated Salivary Gland Disease (Summary Box 54.4): Occurs in 5–10% of HIV patients; presents with painless bilateral multicystic parotid enlargement due to Benign Lymphoepithelial Cysts (BLEC) and Diffuse Infiltrative Lymphocytosis Syndrome (DILS — CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration), mimicking Sjögren’s syndrome but with negative anti-Ro/La autoantibodies.
Recurrent Parotitis of Childhood
children.detail: Rapid recurrent unilateral/bilateral parotid swelling in children aged 3–6 years; sialogram shows characteristic “snowstorm” punctate sialectasis; managed with antibiotics and sialendoscopic washouts (usually resolves spontaneously at puberty).

children.title: Sialadenosis (Sialosis)
children.detail: Non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic, painless bilateral symmetrical parotid enlargement caused by autonomic neuropathy and acinar hypertrophy in chronic alcoholism/cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition/bulimia, and drugs (guanethidine, thioridazine).

children.title: Facial Nerve Injury
children.detail: If transected posterior to a vertical line dropped from the lateral canthus of the eye, perform immediate primary epineurial microsurgical repair (or cable nerve graft). Branches injured anterior to this line have rich cross-anastomoses and do not require repair.

children.title: Stensen’s Duct Injury
children.detail: Repair within 72 hours by primary end-to-end microsurgical anastomosis over a fine Silastic/epidural catheter stent cannulated via the buccal papilla.

children.title: Submandibular Gland Excision (Operative Steps & Nerve Relations — Summary Box 54.6):
Incision
children.detail: Horizontal skin-crease incision two finger-breadths (3–4 cm) below the lower border of the mandible (to avoid the marginal mandibular nerve).

children.title: Three Crucial Nerves Related to the Submandibular Gland
Marginal Mandibular Branch of Facial Nerve
children.detail: Runs in the deep fascia superficial to the facial vein and artery; protected via the Hayes Martin manoeuvre (ligating the facial vein low on the inferior border of the gland and reflecting the tied upper stump superiorly along with the investing fascia). Injury paralyses depressor anguli oris/depressor labii inferioris → drooping/asymmetry of the corner of the mouth on smiling.

children.title: Lingual Nerve
children.detail: Lies on the hyoglossus muscle deep to the mylohyoid; loops beneath Wharton’s duct (“double-crossing” it) and is attached to the deep lobe of the gland via the submandibular ganglion (which must be carefully divided to free the gland). Injury causes ipsilateral loss of general sensation and taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

children.title: Hypoglossal Nerve (CN XII)
children.detail: Runs deep to the gland on the hyoglossus muscle below Wharton’s duct, accompanied by the thin-walled ranine veins. Injury causes ipsilateral tongue hemi-atrophy and deviation of the protruding tongue towards the injured side.

data.title: 6. Chapter 55 & 56: Thyroid & Parathyroid Glands (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Surgical Anatomy of the Thyroid & Parathyroids
Beahrs’ Triangle (for locating the Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve)
children.detail: Bounded by the Common carotid artery (base/laterally), Inferior thyroid artery (superiorly), and Recurrent laryngeal nerve (inferomedially) in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.

children.title: Tubercle of Zuckerkandl
children.detail: Posterolateral pyramidal projection of the thyroid lobe; the RLN almost constantly runs immediately medial/posterior to this tubercle in a fissure between it and the trachea before entering the larynx beneath Berry’s ligament.

children.title: Non-Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (~1–2% on the Right side)
children.detail: Associated with an anomalous retro-oesophageal right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria); arises directly from the cervical vagus and runs transversely into the larynx.

children.title: Pathogenesis in Chronic Kidney Disease
children.detail: Impaired renal phosphate excretion → hyperphosphataemia stimulates osteocytes to secrete Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 (FGF-23), which inhibits renal 1α-hydroxylase → **low 1,25(OH)_2D_3 (calcitriol)** → reduced gut calcium absorption and hypocalcaemia → continuous chief-cell stimulation and four-gland parathyroid hyperplasia (initially diffuse polyclonal, later nodular monoclonal hyperplasia with downregulation of Vitamin D receptors and Calcium-Sensing Receptors, rendering it medically refractory).

children.title: Medical Management
children.detail: Low-phosphate diet, Phosphate binders (Sevelamer, Calcium acetate), Calcitriol/Alfacalcidol, and Cinacalcet (calcimimetic). Renal transplantation is the only definitive cure.

children.title: Indications for Parathyroidectomy in Secondary HPT (Tables 56.3 & 56.4): Intact PTH >500–800 pg/mL with refractory hypercalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia, largest gland volume >500 mm³ (>1 cm), severe renal osteodystrophy/bone pain, intractable pruritus, erythropoietin-resistant anaemia, or Calciphylaxis. Performed via Subtotal (3(1/2)-gland) Parathyroidectomy or Total Parathyroidectomy with Forearm Autotransplantation + Bilateral Cervical Thymectomy.
Casanova Test
children.detail: Used in recurrent hyperparathyroidism after forearm autotransplantation; inflating a tourniquet on the grafted arm or selective brachial venous sampling demonstrating a >20:1 PTH gradient confirms graft-dependent recurrence.

children.title: Calciphylaxis (Calcific Uraemic Arteriolopathy)
children.detail: Life-threatening syndrome (up to 87% mortality from sepsis) in ~4% of dialysis patients with an elevated Calcium × Phosphate product and deficiency of calcification-inhibitor α_2-Heremans–Schmid glycoprotein (Fetuin-A). Causes medial calcification and thrombosis of dermal/subcutaneous arterioles, presenting with excruciatingly painful violaceous retiform purpuric plaques and black necrotic skin eschars on the thighs, legs, and abdomen. Requires urgent parathyroidectomy, sodium thiosulphate, and meticulous wound care.

data.title: 7. Chapter 57: Adrenal Glands & Abdominal Endocrine Disorders (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Defined as an asymptomatic adrenal mass (≥ 1 cm) discovered incidentally on cross-sectional imaging performed for non-adrenal reasons.
Two Questions Must Be Answered in Parallel
Is it Functionally Active? All patients undergo
children.detail: (i) Overnight 1 mg Dexamethasone Suppression Test (cortisol >50 nmol/L indicates autonomous cortisol secretion / Cushing’s), (ii) Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (to exclude Phaeochromocytoma), (iii) Plasma Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR) (if hypertensive or hypokalaemic, to exclude Conn’s syndrome), and (iv) Sex hormones / steroid precursors (DHEAS, testosterone, 17-OH-progesterone if virilisation or adrenocortical carcinoma is suspected).

children.title: Benign Adenoma (Lipid-rich)
children.detail: Size <4 cm, homogeneous, Unenhanced CT attenuation ≤ 10 Hounsfield Units (HU), rapid contrast washout (Absolute washout >60%, Relative washout >40% at 15 minutes), and signal drop on out-of-phase chemical-shift MRI.

children.title: Suspicious for Malignancy
children.detail: Size >4 cm (especially >6 cm), >10 HU density, delayed contrast washout (<60% absolute / <40% relative), no signal loss on chemical-shift MRI, or FDG-PET avidity.

children.title: Indications for Adrenalectomy in Incidentaloma
children.detail: (i) Any hormonally functioning tumour, and (ii) Any non-functioning tumour ≥ 4 cm or with imaging features suspicious for malignancy (Laparoscopic if <6 cm without local invasion; Open radical adrenalectomy if >6 cm or locally invasive).

children.title: Pathology
children.detail: 30–40% unilateral Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma (APA) (small 1–2 cm golden-yellow “canary tumour” arising in the zona glomerulosa; 40% harbour somatic KCNJ5 potassium-channel mutations) vs 60% Bilateral Idiopathic Adrenal Hyperplasia (and rare Familial Hyperaldosteronism Types I–IV; Type I is Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism treated with low-dose dexamethasone).

children.title: Clinical Features
children.detail: Commonest cause of secondary/endocrine hypertension; causes drug-resistant hypertension, sodium retention, and hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (muscle weakness, cramps, polyuria/polydipsia from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; note that >50% are normokalaemic at presentation).

children.title: Screening
children.detail: Elevated Plasma Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR >850 suggestive, >1700 diagnostic) after stopping spironolactone/eplerenone and ACE inhibitors for 2–4 weeks and correcting hypokalaemia.

children.title: Confirmatory Test
children.detail: Saline infusion test, oral salt-loading test, or fludrocortisone suppression test.

children.title: Subtype Lateralisation (Unilateral APA vs Bilateral Hyperplasia)
children.detail: High-resolution adrenal CT followed by Adrenal Vein Sampling (AVS — Gold Standard in patients >35 years) or ¹¹C-Metomidate PET-CT.

children.title: Unilateral APA
children.detail: Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy (after preoperative blood pressure and potassium normalization with Spironolactone).

children.title: Bilateral Adrenal Hyperplasia
children.detail: Lifelong medical therapy with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (Spironolactone or Eplerenone — avoids gynaecomastia).

children.title: Etiology
children.detail: ACTH-Dependent (80–85%): Pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing’s Disease — 70–80%) or Ectopic ACTH Syndrome (10%) (small-cell lung cancer, bronchial/thymic/pancreatic NETs); ACTH-Independent (15–20%): Unilateral Adrenocortical Adenoma, Adrenocortical Carcinoma, or Primary Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH).

children.title: Clinical Features (Summary Box 57.2): Central truncal obesity, moon-like plethoric face, interscapular “buffalo hump”, supraclavicular fat pads, proximal myopathy (“lemon on sticks”), wide purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, hirsutism, acne, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and psychosis/depression.
Confirm Hypercortisolism (Requires ≥ 2 abnormal first-line tests)
children.detail: (i) Overnight 1 mg Dexamethasone Suppression Test (8 am cortisol >50 nmol/L), (ii) Late-night salivary cortisol (loss of circadian nadir), and (iii) 24-hour Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC) (>3 × upper limit).

children.title: Suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL)
children.detail: Adrenal Cushing’s → perform Adrenal CT/MRI.

children.title: Normal/Elevated ACTH
children.detail: Pituitary vs Ectopic → perform Pituitary MRI, High-dose (8 mg) DST, and Bilateral Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (BIPSS) (or CT Thorax + ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT for ectopic ACTH).

children.title: Preoperative Medical Control
children.detail: Steroidogenesis inhibitors (Metyrapone, Ketoconazole, or IV Etomidate in life-threatening hypercortisolaemic crisis) + DVT and antibiotic prophylaxis.

children.title: Surgery
children.detail: Trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy for Cushing’s disease; Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy for unilateral adrenal adenoma.

children.title: Mandatory Postoperative Corticosteroid Replacement
children.detail: Because chronic hypercortisolism suppresses hypothalamic CRH/pituitary ACTH and causes atrophy of the contralateral adrenal cortex, all patients undergoing unilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing’s require intraoperative and postoperative Hydrocortisone replacement (weaned slowly over 6–12 months once a Short Synacthen Test confirms recovery of the contralateral gland).

children.title: Nelson’s Syndrome
children.detail: Occurs in 10% of patients with Cushing’s disease who undergo bilateral adrenalectomy; loss of cortisol negative feedback causes rapid enlargement of the pituitary corticotroph tumour with massive ACTH and POMC/MSH secretion, causing intense cutaneous hyperpigmentation and visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia).

children.title: Rare (1–2 per million), highly aggressive malignancy; 60% are functional (rapidly progressive Cushing’s syndrome + Virilisation in women due to co-secretion of cortisol and DHEAS/androgens).
Pathology
children.detail: Large (>6–10 cm), invasive tumours; histological malignancy is assessed by the Modified Weiss Score (≥ 3 indicates malignancy) and Ki-67 index (>10% high risk).

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Open En Bloc Radical Adrenalectomy (resecting adjacent kidney, spleen, distal pancreas, or liver wall if invaded to achieve R0 margins) + Adjuvant Mitotane (adrenolytic drug; requires concurrent hydrocortisone replacement) ± EDP (Etoposide, Doxorubicin, Cisplatin) chemotherapy.

children.title: Rule of 90s
children.detail: 90% are benign, 90% are solitary, 90% are <2 cm, and equally distributed across the head, body, and tail of the pancreas; 10% are associated with MEN 1 (often multiple).

children.title: Symptoms and signs of neuroglycopenia/hypoglycaemia precipitated by fasting or exercise (confusion, visual disturbances, bizarre behaviour, seizures, coma, sweating, palpitations; patients gain weight because they eat frequently to prevent attacks).
Documented plasma glucose <3.0 mmol/L (<50 mg/dL) at the time of symptoms.
Immediate relief of symptoms upon oral or IV administration of glucose.
Biochemical Confirmation (Supervised 72-Hour Fast Test — Gold Standard)
children.detail: Concomitant blood glucose <2.5–3.0 mmol/L + inappropriately elevated serum Insulin (>6 μU/mL) + elevated C-Peptide (>0.2 nmol/L) and Proinsulin, with negative sulfonylurea screen (elevated C-peptide rules out factitious exogenous insulin administration, where C-peptide is suppressed).

children.title: Localisation
children.detail: Pancreatic protocol CT/MRI + Endoscopic Ultrasonography (EUS — >90% sensitive) + Intra-arterial Calcium Stimulation with Hepatic Venous Sampling (for occult/MEN 1 lesions) or GLP-1 receptor PET-CT.

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: Preoperative Diazoxide (inhibits insulin release from β-cells) and frequent carbohydrate meals → Laparoscopic or Open Surgical Enucleation (with intraoperative ultrasound to confirm the tumour is >2–3 mm away from the main pancreatic duct; distal pancreatectomy if in the tail or MEN 1).

children.title: Pathology
children.detail: Gastrin-secreting NET causing massive gastric acid hypersecretion; 60–90% are malignant; 20–25% occur as part of MEN 1. 70–80% are actually located in the submucosa of the first/second part of the Duodenum (small <1 cm and multiple in MEN 1) rather than the pancreas.

children.title: Passaro’s Gastrinoma Triangle (Houses 90% of Gastrinomas)
children.detail: Bounded superiorly by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, inferiorly by the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum, and medially by the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas.

children.title: Clinical Features
children.detail: Severe, refractory, multiple peptic ulcers in atypical sites (distal duodenum/jejunum) + chronic secretory diarrhoea and steatorrhoea (high gastric acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates bile salts; diarrhoea resolves with nasogastric aspiration).

children.title: Diagnosis
children.detail: Fasting Serum Gastrin (FSG) >10 × normal (>1000 pg/mL) in the presence of basal gastric pH <2.0. If FSG is borderline (100–1000 pg/mL), perform a Secretin Stimulation Test (provokes a paradoxical rise in serum gastrin >200 pg/mL in gastrinoma). Localised by ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT (SSTR-PET) and EUS. Always screen for MEN 1 (serum calcium/PTH).

children.title: Treatment
children.detail: High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitors (Omeprazole/Pantoprazole) + Surgical resection/duodenotomy with peripancreatic lymph node dissection for sporadic gastrinomas (in MEN 1, parathyroidectomy is performed first, and surgery is reserved for pancreatic tumours >2 cm).

children.title: VIPoma (Verner–Morrison / WDHA Syndrome)
children.detail: Secretes Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide → Watery Diarrhoea (profuse tea-coloured secretory diarrhoea >3–5 L/day), Hypokalaemia, and Achlorhydria (“Pancreatic Cholera”); treated with Octreotide, fluid/electrolyte resuscitation, and distal pancreatectomy.

children.title: Glucagonoma (α-cell tumour)
children.detail: Causes the “4 D’s”: Dermatitis (pathognomonic Necrolytic Migratory Erythema around perineum/perioral/extremities), Diabetes mellitus, Deep vein thrombosis, and Depression/Weight loss + painful glossitis/stomatitis and normocytic anaemia.

children.title: Somatostatinoma (δ-cell tumour)
children.detail: Classic triad of Diabetes mellitus + Cholelithiasis (gallstones) + Steatorrhoea/Diarrhoea; duodenal periampullary somatostatinomas contain psammoma bodies and are associated with NF-1.

children.title: Non-Functioning P-NETs (NF-P-NETs — 60–90% of all P-NETs; Fig 57.16): Express Chromogranin A, Synaptophysin, and Pancreatic Polypeptide (PP) without a hormonal syndrome. Asymptomatic Grade 1 tumours <2 cm can be safely observed with serial EUS/MRI; tumours >2 cm or symptomatic/Grade 2 require surgical resection.
1. Gastric NETs (3 Types arising from Enterochromaffin-like [ECL] cells)
Type I (70–80%)
children.detail: Multiple small (<1 cm), benign polyps associated with chronic autoimmune atrophic gastritis / pernicious anaemia (achlorhydria → high gastric pH → hypergastrinaemia drives ECL hyperplasia); treated conservatively with endoscopic surveillance/polypectomy.

children.title: Type II (5%)
children.detail: Multiple small polyps secondary to Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome / MEN 1 (low gastric pH + high gastrin).

children.title: Type III (15–20%)
children.detail: Sporadic, solitary, large (>2 cm) infiltrative tumour with normal gastrin levels; behaves aggressively like gastric adenocarcinoma → requires radical gastrectomy + lymphadenectomy.

children.title: Arise from Kulchitsky (enterochromaffin) cells in the terminal ileum (30% are multifocal). Secrete 5-Hydroxytryptamine (Serotonin), Substance P, Kallikrein, and Histamine.
Desmoplastic Mesenteric Reaction
children.detail: Nodal metastases at the root of the mesentery release serotonin and growth factors that induce intense retroperitoneal fibrosis, drawing in and kinking bowel loops and constricting the superior mesenteric vessels (“spoke-wheel / sunburst” appearance on CT — Fig 57.18), causing chronic postprandial mesenteric ischaemia and small bowel obstruction.

children.title: Carcinoid Syndrome (Occurs in 20–30%, ONLY when liver metastases or retroperitoneal/bronchial primaries bypass hepatic first-pass monoamine oxidase degradation of serotonin):

Episodic Cutaneous Flushing (90%) of face/neck, Secretory Watery Diarrhoea (70%), abdominal cramps, Bronchospasm/Wheezing, telangiectasia, pellagra (niacin/tryptophan depletion), and Carcinoid Heart Disease (Hedinger’s Syndrome): Endocardial fibrosis producing Tricuspid Regurgitation and Pulmonary Stenosis (right-sided heart valves; left heart valves are spared because pulmonary endothelial monoamine oxidase inactivates serotonin).
Diagnosis
children.detail: Elevated serum Chromogranin A + elevated 24-hour Urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) + Contrast CT/MRI + ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATOC / DOTATATE PET-CT + Echocardiography.

children.title: Medical / Perioperative Cover
children.detail: Long-acting Somatostatin Analogues (Octreotide LAR or Lanreotide) control flushing/diarrhoea and exert an antiproliferative effect (mandatory IV Octreotide infusion during anaesthesia/surgery to prevent a fatal Carcinoid Crisis — profound hypotension, bronchospasm, and arrhythmias). Second-line systemic therapy for metastatic disease is Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) using ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE or Everolimus.

children.title: Surgical
children.detail: Radical resection of the small bowel primary, mesenteric nodal mass (preserving SMA branches), synchronous liver metastasectomy/RFA, and prophylactic cholecystectomy (because long-term Octreotide causes gallstones).

children.title: 3. Appendiceal NETs (Commonest tumour of the appendix)
Found incidentally at the tip of the appendix in 0.3–0.5% of appendicectomies.
<1 cm
children.detail: Simple Appendicectomy alone is 100% curative (no follow-up needed).

children.title: 1–2 cm
children.detail: Appendicectomy is sufficient unless high-risk features are present (positive base margin, deep mesoappendiceal invasion >3 mm, Grade 2/3, or lymphovascular invasion), which warrant a right hemicolectomy.

children.title: >2 cm
children.detail: Perform a formal Oncological Right Hemicolectomy.

data.title: 8. Chapter 58, 61 & 62: Breast, Arterial & Venous Disorders (Remaining Topics)

children.title: Poland’s Syndrome
children.detail: Congenital unilateral absence of the sternocostal head of Pectoralis Major, hypoplasia/absence of the breast and nipple (amazia/athelia), deficiency of subcutaneous fat, costal cartilage defects (ribs 2–4), and ipsilateral symbrachydactyly (short, webbed fingers).

children.title: Mondor’s Disease [TU]
children.detail: Superficial thrombophlebitis of the thoracoepigastric or lateral thoracic vein of the breast and anterior chest wall (idiopathic or post-biopsy/trauma). Presents with acute linear pain and a palpable, tender, subcutaneous cord-like structure that forms a characteristic vertical skin groove/furrow (“bowstring sign”) when the arm is raised. Self-limiting within 4–6 weeks; treated with reassurance and NSAIDs (after mammogram excludes occult cancer).

children.title: Paget’s Disease of the Nipple
children.detail: Eczematous, crusted, weeping erosion of the nipple that destroys the nipple and spreads onto the areola (unlike benign eczema, it is unilateral, destroys the nipple apex first, does not itch severely, and fails to respond to topical steroids). Histologically characterised by large, pale, vacuolated intraepidermal adenocarcinoma cells (Paget cells) derived from underlying DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma (present in >95%). Diagnosed by wedge/punch biopsy of the nipple + mammography/MRI; treated by central cone excision + radiotherapy (if confined to retroareolar DCIS) or Mastectomy + SLNB.

children.title: Breast Cancer in Pregnancy
children.detail: Often presents late with aggressive TNBC biology. USG and core biopsy are safe (mammogram with fetal shielding is safe; avoid gadolinium MRI, CT, and bone scans). Surgery (MRM) is safe in all trimesters (BCS is only feasible in the 3rd trimester when radiotherapy can be given postpartum). Chemotherapy (Anthracyclines/Taxanes) is contraindicated in the 1st trimester (teratogenic during organogenesis) but safe in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters (stopped at 34 weeks). Radiotherapy, Tamoxifen, and Trastuzumab are strictly contraindicated throughout pregnancy.

children.title: Male Breast Cancer
children.detail: Accounts for <0.5–1% of breast cancers; associated with BRCA2 mutations and Klinefelter’s syndrome (47,XXY). Presents in elderly men as a painless, hard subareolar lump with early invasion of the nipple–areola complex, skin ulceration, and pectoralis major fixation (due to scant breast parenchyma). >90% are ER-positive; treated with Modified Radical Mastectomy (or Simple mastectomy + SLNB), adjuvant radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and Tamoxifen for 5–10 years.

children.title: Breast Angiosarcoma
children.detail: Highly lethal mesenchymal malignancy arising either de novo in young women or secondary to breast-conserving radiotherapy / chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema (Stewart–Treves syndrome) 5–10 years after treatment; presents as a bruised-looking purple skin plaque/nodule; treated by wide mastectomy.

children.title: Atheromatous plaque at the carotid bifurcation / origin of the Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) embolises platelet-fibrin thrombi (Hollenhorst cholesterol crystals in retinal arteries), causing ipsilateral Amaurosis Fugax (transient monocular blindness — “curtain coming down over one eye”), contralateral hemiparesis/hemisensory TIA or stroke, or dysphasia.
Indication for Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA) (NASCET / ECST Trials)
children.detail: Symptomatic patients with 50–99% ICA stenosis on Duplex USG/CTA, ideally performed within 2 weeks of the index TIA/minor stroke (preserving the hypoglossal, vagus, glossopharyngeal, and marginal mandibular nerves and closing the arteriotomy with a patch angioplasty using a temporary intraluminal shunt).

children.title: Subclavian Steal Syndrome
children.detail: Proximal occlusion/stenosis of the first part of the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery. Exercising the ipsilateral arm lowers arm vascular resistance, causing retrograde blood flow down the ipsilateral vertebral artery (“stealing” blood from the basilar/vertebrobasilar cerebral circulation) → arm claudication + vertebrobasilar syncope, vertigo, ataxia, and visual disturbances on arm exercise, accompanied by a >20 mmHg blood pressure discrepancy between the two arms. Treated by subclavian angioplasty and stenting or carotid–subclavian bypass.

children.title: Commonest peripheral arterial aneurysm (70%); 50% are bilateral and 30–40% have a coexisting Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm.

Rarely ruptures; instead, it presents with limb-threatening acute thrombosis or chronic distal thromboembolism (“trash foot”) that progressively occludes the crural run-off vessels (carrying a 50% amputation rate once acute thrombosis occurs).
Indications for Elective Repair
children.detail: Any symptomatic popliteal aneurysm, or any asymptomatic popliteal aneurysm ≥ 2.0 cm in diameter (especially if lined with mural thrombus). Repaired via Medial approach proximal-and-distal ligation + reversed GSV Exclusion Bypass or Posterior approach inlay graft repair.

children.title: Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis
children.detail: Granulomatous arteritis of medium/large cranial branches in patients >50 years causing unilateral throbbing headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, tender pulseless cord-like superficial temporal artery, and ESR >50 mm/h. Immediate high-dose oral/IV Prednisolone must be started before temporal artery biopsy to prevent irreversible blindness from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (ophthalmic artery occlusion).

children.title: Takayasu’s Arteritis (“Pulseless Disease”)
children.detail: Pan-arteritis of the aortic arch and its major branches in young Asian women (<40 years), leading to absent upper limb pulses, hypertension (renal artery stenosis), and ocular/cerebral ischaemia.

children.title: Cystic Myxomatous Adventitial Degeneration
children.detail: Accumulation of mucinous synovial-like jelly within the adventitia of the popliteal artery in young non-smoking men, compressing the lumen to cause intermittent claudication (Ishikawa’s sign: pedal pulses disappear on sharp knee flexion); treated by evacuation or interposition vein graft.

children.title: Pelvic Congestion Syndrome (PCS)
children.detail: Chronic non-cyclical dull pelvic ache, dyspareunia, and vulval/perineal/posterior thigh varicosities in multiparous premenopausal women caused by incompetence of the ovarian (gonadal) and internal iliac veins; diagnosed by transvaginal duplex/MR venography and treated by percutaneous transcatheter ovarian vein coil embolisation.

children.title: Effort Axillary–Subclavian Vein Thrombosis (Paget–Schrötter Syndrome)
children.detail: Primary thrombosis of the axillary/subclavian vein in young athletes/weightlifters following repetitive overhead arm exertion due to venous thoracic outlet compression at the costoclavicular space (between the first rib, subclavius muscle/costoclavicular ligament, and clavicle, or a cervical rib). Presents with an acutely swollen, aching, cyanosed arm and dilated shoulder collaterals. Treated by urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by surgical thoracic outlet decompression (First Rib Resection) and anticoagulation.

children.title: Venous Trauma & Venous Tumours
children.detail: Major axial venous injuries (especially the popliteal vein and IVC) should be repaired (via lateral venorrhaphy, vein patch, Carrel triangulation end-to-end anastomosis, or autologous panel/spiral saphenous vein graft) rather than ligated to prevent severe venous hypertension and limb loss, accompanied by calf fasciotomy if combined with arterial injury. Leiomyosarcoma of the Inferior Vena Cava is the commonest primary malignant venous tumour (presents with Budd–Chiari syndrome or lower limb oedema; treated by radical resection and prosthetic graft reconstruction).

children.title: 1. Why it looks "short" on screen, but is actually massive in content
Word & Page Count
children.detail: The file you pasted contains ~16,500 words. When pasted into Microsoft Word (Times New Roman, 12 pt, 1.25 spacing, single column) along with the 12 tables and 30 textbook figures, it comes out to 48 to 55 pages.

children.title: Why is it 50 pages instead of 210 pages (the length of the 11 textbook chapters)?
Bailey & Love is written in narrative paragraphs with historical anecdotes, case stories, and conversational filler.

Your notes strip out 100% of the conversational fluff and convert every paragraph into direct marking-scheme bullet points and side-headings (Definition, Etiopathogenesis, Pathology, Clinical Features, Investigations, Management, Complications).
The Physics of a 3-Hour Surgery Exam

In a 3-hour theory exam, a student can physically handwrite at most 3,500 to 4,000 words total (~400–500 words for a Long Essay, ~150–200 words for a Short Essay, and ~75–100 words for a Short Answer).
Every Long Essay and Short Essay in your notes already contains 400 to 900 words of pure, high-yield points—which is more than you can physically write in the exam hall.
If you haven't read the textbook yet and have limited time
children.detail: Trying to read 210 pages of dense 2-column Bailey & Love text for the first time will cause severe information overload, and you will struggle to recall structured headings during the exam. Studying structured, side-headed notes is the fastest and safest way to score distinction marks on a first read.
